Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 27, verses 1–3:

Surat an-Naml (The Ant)
Ninety-three, or four, or five verses; Meccan

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Ta, Sin. These are the verses of the Qur'an and a Book that makes things clear.﴾ ﴿A guidance and good tidings for the believers.﴾ ﴿Those who establish the prayer, pay the zakat, and are certain of the Hereafter.﴾

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Ta, Sin. These are the verses of the Qur'an and a Book that makes things clear.﴾ ﴿A guidance and good tidings for the believers.﴾ ﴿Those who establish the prayer, pay the zakat, and are certain of the Hereafter.﴾

Know that His saying ﴿Tilka﴾ ("These") is a pointing to the verses of the surah, and al-Kitab al-Mubin ("the Clear Book") is the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz). Its clarity lies in that everything that exists has been inscribed in it, so the angels who look into it make clear the existing things. He made al-Kitab al-Mubin indefinite (nakkara) so that it would be vague through indefiniteness, and thus more majestic for it, like His saying: ﴿In a seat of truth, in the presence of a Sovereign, All-Powerful.﴾ [al-Qamar: 55]. Ibn Abi Abla read (wa-Kitabun mubinun) in the nominative, on the reckoning of "wa-ayatu kitabin mubin," so the genitive noun was deleted and the noun in the genitive was put in its place. If you ask: what is the difference between this and His saying: ﴿Alif, Lam, Ra. These are the verses of the Book and a Qur'an that makes things clear.﴾ [al-Hijr: 1]? I say: there is no difference, because the conjunctive waw does not require sequence.

As for His saying ﴿A guidance and good tidings for the believers﴾, it is in a position of accusative or nominative. The accusative is as a circumstantial state (hal), meaning guiding and bringing good tidings, and the governing element in it is the sense of pointing contained in "tilka." The nominative has three possibilities: in the sense of "they are guidance and good tidings"; as an apposition (badal) to "ayat"; and as a second predicate after a predicate, meaning its verses combined the verses of the Book and that they are guidance and good tidings.

The scholars differed on the reason for restricting guidance to the believers, in two ways:

The first: the meaning is that it guides them to Paradise, and it is good tidings for them, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So He will admit them into mercy from Himself and bounty, and guide them to Himself on a straight path.﴾ [an-Nisa: 175]. For this reason it is specific to the believers.

The second: the meaning of guidance is indication (al-dalala). Then they mentioned several reasons for restricting it to the believers:

One of them: He restricted it to the believers because He mentioned good tidings along with guidance, and good tidings are only for the believers.

The second: the reason for the restriction is that they held fast to it, so He singled them out by mention, as in His saying: ﴿You are only a warner to those who fear it.﴾ [an-Nazi'at: 45].

The third: the meaning of its being guidance for the believers is that it increases their guidance, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And Allah increases in guidance those who are guided.﴾ [Maryam: 76].

Page 153

As for His saying ﴿Those who establish the prayer﴾, the closest view is that it refers to the five daily prayers, because the definition by the article "al" (al-alif wa-l-lam) requires that. Establishing the prayer means performing it with its conditions. The same applies to zakat, which is the obligatory zakat; establishing it means placing it with those who are entitled to it.

As for His saying ﴿and are certain of the Hereafter﴾, there is a question about it: the believers who establish the prayer and pay zakat must necessarily be certain of the Hereafter, so what is the purpose of mentioning it again? Its answer is in two ways:

The first: that it is part of the relative clause (silat al-mawsul). Then there are two views:

The first: the perfection of a human being lies in knowing the Truth for its own sake, and knowing the report for the sake of acting upon it. As for knowledge of the Truth, it has many divisions, but what is derived from it as the path to salvation is knowledge of the Origin (al-mabda') and knowledge of the Return (al-ma'ad). As for the good that is acted upon, it has many divisions, and the most noble of them are two: obedience with the self and obedience with wealth. So His saying ﴿for the believers﴾ refers to knowledge of the Origin; His saying ﴿who establish the prayer and pay zakat﴾ refers to obedience with the self and wealth; and His saying ﴿and are certain of the Hereafter﴾ refers to knowledge of the Return. It is as if He, glorified and exalted, made knowledge of the Origin the first extreme, knowledge of the Return the final extreme, and placed obedience with self and wealth in the middle between them.

The second: the believers who establish the prayer and pay zakat include some who are firmly convinced of resurrection and gathering, and some who are doubtful about it but perform these acts of worship as a precaution, saying: if I am right in them, I have attained happiness; and if I am wrong in them, I have lost only a few goods in this brief period. Whoever prays and pays zakat in this manner is not, in reality, guided by the Qur'an. But whoever is firmly certain of the Hereafter is guided by it. For this reason He mentioned this condition.

The second: that His saying ﴿and are certain of the Hereafter﴾ be taken as a parenthetical clause (jumla i'tiradiyya), as if it were said: those who believe and do righteous deeds, through establishing the prayer and giving zakat, are the ones who are certain of the Hereafter. This is the closer view, and it is indicated by the fact that He formed an independent nominal sentence and repeated in it the subject, which is "hum," until its meaning becomes: none are certain of the Hereafter with true certainty except these who combine faith and righteous action, because fear of the consequence drives them to bear hardships.

The commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 27, verses 4–5:

God, exalted is He, says: ﴿Indeed, those who do not believe in the Hereafter – We have made their deeds appealing to them, so they wander blindly.﴾ ﴿Those are the ones for whom is the worst torment, and they in the Hereafter are the greatest losers.﴾

Know that when God, exalted is He, had explained what the believers would receive of good tidings, He followed it with what the disbelievers would suffer of evil punishment. So He said: ﴿Indeed, those who do not believe in the Hereafter – We have made their deeds appealing to them﴾. People have differed over how He attributed the adornment of their deeds to Himself, when He attributed it to Satan in His saying: ﴿So Satan made their deeds appealing to them﴾ [al-Nahl: 63]. As for our companions (the Ash'aris), they took the verse at face value. This is because a person does not do anything at all unless a motivator calls him to the act, and what is understood by the motivator is knowledge, belief, or supposition that the act contains some benefit. This motivator must be from the act of God, exalted is He, for two reasons:

The first: If it were from the act of the servant, it would require another motivator for it, and this would lead to an infinite regress (tasalsul), which is impossible.

The second: Knowledge is either necessary (daruri) or acquired (kasbi). If it is necessary, then it requires two conceptions (tasawwurayn), and conception cannot be acquired. For the one who acquires it, if he is aware of it, then he already conceives it, and acquiring what is already acquired is impossible. And if he is not aware of it, he would be heedless of it, and the one who is heedless of a thing cannot be seeking it. If you say: "It is known from one aspect and not known from another," I say: "What is known is other than what is not known, so the earlier division returns in each of these two aspects." Since it is established that conception is not acquired at all, and that necessary knowledge is that in which the presence of each of its two conceptions is sufficient for the occurrence of assent (tasdiq), then conceptions are not acquired, and they necessitate assents. Therefore, whenever the conceptions occur, assent occurs without doubt, and whenever they do not occur, assent does not occur at all. So the occurrence of these self-evident assents is not by acquisition. Then, if the self-evident assents necessitate the theoretical assents, the theoretical assents are not acquired, because the necessary consequence of the necessary is necessary. And if they do not necessitate them, then those things which we supposed to be theoretical knowledge are not so, but rather they are imitative beliefs (i'tiqadat taqlidiyya), because there is no meaning to the belief of the imitator except a beautifying belief that he performs from the outset without there being any cause for it. Thus it is established that all knowledge is necessary, and it is established that the principles of acts are knowledge. Therefore all the acts of servants are necessary, and the human being is compelled in the form of one who chooses. So it is established that God, exalted is He, is the One who made the deed of every doer appealing to him. The meaning of the adornment (tazyin) is that He creates in his heart knowledge of the benefits and pleasures it contains, and He does not create in his heart knowledge of the harms and calamities it contains. By these decisive rational proofs, it has been established that this verse must be taken at face value.

As for the Mu'tazila (the Mu'tazila, a rationalist school), they gave several interpretations of it:

The first: The meaning is that We made clear to them the matter of religion and what they must hold fast to, and We adorned it by making its goodness clear to them and the reward they would have in it. This is because God's adornment of the deed is nothing but describing it as good, obligatory, and having a praiseworthy outcome. This is what is meant by His saying: ﴿God has endeared to you faith and made it beautiful in your hearts﴾ [al-Hujurat: 7]. And the meaning of ﴿so they wander blindly﴾ indicates this, because the meaning is: they deviate and turn away from what We made appealing of their deeds.

The second: When God gave them long life and abundant provision, they made God's bounty upon them a means toward following their desires and not submitting to the obligations that fall upon them. So it is as if God adorned their deeds by that. To this points the statement of the angels, peace be upon them, in His saying: ﴿But You gave them and their fathers enjoyment until they forgot the remembrance﴾ [al-Furqan: 18].

The third: His granting respite to Satan and leaving him free until he makes their deeds appealing to them is an evident association with the adornment, so it was attributed to Him.

As for the answer to the first: His saying ﴿their deeds﴾ is a general expression requiring that God made all their deeds appealing to them, whether the deed was good or ugly. The meaning of adornment has already been mentioned.

As for the answer to the second: When God gave them long life and abundant provision, is it the case that these things have an effect in making the act of disobedience preferred over abandoning it, or do they have no effect in it? If the first, then we have shown that preponderance, whenever it occurs, must reach the level of necessitation, and then the purpose is achieved; and if they have no effect, then these things in relation to their deeds are like the creaking of a door and the cawing of a crow, and that prevents attributing their act to them. This very answer applies to the third interpretation they mentioned. And God knows best.

As for His saying ﴿so they wander blindly﴾: al-'Ama (wandering) is bewilderment and hesitation, as is the condition of one who is lost from the path.

As for His saying: ﴿Those are the ones for whom is the worst torment﴾, there are two views on it:

The first: It is killing and capture on the day of Badr.

The second: It is the absolute torment, whether in this world or the Hereafter, and what is meant by "evil" (su') is its severity and magnitude.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿and they in the Hereafter are the greatest losers﴾, there are two views on it:

The first: There is no loss greater than that a person loses himself, by being deprived of health and well-being in this world and being delivered to the great torment in the Hereafter.

The second: What is meant is that they lost their dwellings in Paradise, had they obeyed. For there is no accountable person except that a dwelling in Paradise is assigned to him, had he obeyed. So when he disobeys, it is transferred to another, and thus he has lost that dwelling.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 27, verses 6–9:**

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And indeed, you are receiving the Qur'an from the Wise, the All-Knowing.﴾ ﴿When Moses said to his family, "Indeed, I have perceived a fire. I will bring you from it some news, or bring you a burning brand that you may warm yourselves."﴾ ﴿But when he came to it, he was called, "Blessed is whoever is in the fire and whoever is around it. And exalted is Allah, Lord of the worlds."﴾ ﴿"O Moses, indeed it is I, Allah, the Exalted in Might, the Wise."﴾

As for His saying, ﴿And indeed, you are receiving the Qur'an from the Wise, the All-Knowing﴾, its meaning is: you are being given it and receiving it from the presence of a Wise One and an All-Knowing One. This is the meaning of their coming in indefinite form (nakiratayn). This verse is a foundation and a preface for the stories that He wishes to relate after it. The word ﴿idh﴾ ("when") is in the accusative case, governed by an implied verb, which is "remember" (udhkur). It is as if He said: "Following that, take the story of Moses as one of the traces of His wisdom and knowledge." It is also permissible for it to be governed by "All-Knowing" (ʿalim). If it is asked: "Wisdom is either the same as knowledge, and knowledge is either included within it. Since He mentioned wisdom, why did He mention knowledge?" The answer: wisdom is knowledge of practical matters only, and knowledge is more general than it, because knowledge may be practical and may be theoretical, and theoretical sciences are more noble than practical sciences. So He mentioned wisdom, which includes the practical sciences, then mentioned "the All-Knowing" (al-ʿAlim), who is one who has attained perfection in knowledge. Perfection of knowledge is attained from three aspects: its unity, the comprehensiveness of its relation to all known things, and its remaining preserved from all changes. These three perfections are found only in the knowledge of Him, glorified and exalted is He.

Know that Allah, the Exalted, mentioned in this surah several kinds of stories.

The first story: the story of Moses, peace be upon him.

As for His saying, ﴿When Moses said to his family﴾, it indicates that with Moses, peace be upon him, there was no one except his wife, the daughter of Shuʿayb, peace be upon him. Allah, the Exalted, referred to her by the term "family" (ahl), and what follows this is the address being in the plural form, which is His saying ﴿Stay﴾ (imkthu).

As for His saying, ﴿Indeed, I have perceived a fire﴾, the meaning is that the two of them were travelling at night, the path had become confused for them, and it was a time of cold. In such a situation the soul is comforted by seeing a fire from a distance, because there is hope in it of removing the confusion about the path and of benefiting from the fire for warming oneself (iṣṭilaʾ). Therefore he gave them good news, saying: ﴿Indeed, I have perceived a fire﴾. The scholars differed. Some said: the intended meaning is "I saw and beheld." Others said: rather, the intended meaning is "I encountered and found, and so I was comforted by it." The first is closer, because they do not distinguish between the speaker's saying "I was comforted by my sight" and "I saw with my sight."

As for His saying, ﴿I will bring you from it some news﴾, "news" (khabar) is that which is reported about the state of the path, because he had gone astray. Then there is an omission in the speech, which is that when he saw the fire he headed towards it and said: ﴿I will bring you from it some news﴾, by which he would know the path.

As for His saying, ﴿or bring you a burning brand (shihab qabas)﴾, "shihab" is a flame, and "qabas" is a fire taken from another fire. He attributed "shihab" to "qabas" because it may be a qabas or not a qabas. Whoever reads it with tanwin (nunation) makes "qabas" a substitute (badal) or a qualifier for what is in it of the meaning of "qabas". Then here there are questions:

The first question: ﴿I will bring you from it some news﴾ and ﴿Perhaps I will bring you from it some news﴾ seem to contradict each other, because one indicates hope and the other certainty. We say: its answer is that the one who hopes, when his hope is strong, may say "I will do such-and-such and it will be such-and-such" while allowing for the possibility of failure.

The second question: why did he use the future particle of postponement (sin al-tasweef)? The answer: it is a promise from him to his family that he will bring it to them, even if he is slow or the distance is great.

The third question: why did he put "or" (aw) between the two matters, and why did he not combine them, since he needed both together? The answer: he based his hope on the fact that if he did not obtain these two aims, he would obtain one of them: either guidance to the path, or taking a fire-brand, trusting in the custom of Allah, the Exalted, because He hardly combines two deprivations upon His servant.

* * *

As for His saying, the Exalted, ﴿so that you may warm yourselves﴾, the meaning is "in order that you may warm yourselves." This indicates that they had a need for warming themselves, and in that case this can only be in a time of cold.

* * *

As for His saying, the Exalted, ﴿He was called, "Blessed is whoever is in the fire and whoever is around it. And exalted is Allah, Lord of the worlds."﴾, there are several discussions in it:

The first discussion: that ﴿an﴾ (that) is explanatory (mufassira), because the calling (nida') contains the meaning of saying. The meaning is: it was said to him, "Blessed."

The second discussion: scholars differed about "whoever is in the fire," in several ways:

One of them: ﴿That Blessed﴾ means "Exalted" (tabāraka), and "the fire" means "the light." The meaning is: Exalted is whoever is in the light, and that is Allah, glorified is He. ﴿And whoever is around it﴾ means the angels. This is related from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, although we are certain that this report is fabricated and invented.

The second: ﴿whoever is in the fire﴾ is the light of Allah, and ﴿whoever is around it﴾ is the angels. This is related from Qatadah and al-Zajjaj.

The third: that Allah, the Exalted, called to him with a speech which he heard from the tree in the blessed place. So the tree was the locus of the speech, and Allah is the One who spoke to him, meaning that His action was in it and not in the tree. Then the tree was in the fire, and around it were angels; therefore He said: ﴿Blessed is whoever is in the fire and whoever is around it﴾. This is the view of al-Jubbaʾi.

The fourth: ﴿whoever is in the fire﴾ is Moses, peace be upon him, because of his nearness to it, and ﴿whoever is around it﴾ means the angels. This is closer, because someone near a thing may be said to be in it.

The fifth: the saying of the author of al-Kashshaf: ﴿Blessed is whoever is in the fire﴾, i.e., whoever is in the place of the fire, and whoever is around the place of it, which is the blessed spot mentioned in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿from the right side of the valley, in the blessed spot﴾ [al-Qasas: 30]. Evidence for this is the reading of Ubayy: "Blessed be the earth and whoever is around it," and also from him: "Blessed be the fire."

The third discussion: the reason for which the spot was blessed, and whoever is in it and around it was blessed, is the occurrence in it of this great matter, which is Allah's speaking to Moses, peace be upon him, and His appointing him as a messenger and manifesting miracles upon him. For this reason Allah made the land of Syria marked with blessings, in His saying: ﴿And We delivered him and Lot to the land which We have blessed for the worlds﴾ [al-Anbiya: 71]. It was fitting that it should be so, for it is the place where the prophets, may the blessings of Allah be upon them, were sent, the descent place of revelation, and their gathering place, whether living or dead.

The fourth discussion: that He, glorified is He, made this speech a preface to Moses' intimate conversation (munajah), peace be upon him. So His saying, ﴿Blessed is whoever is in the fire and whoever is around it﴾, indicates that a great matter has been decreed, from which blessing spreads throughout the entire land of Syria. As for His saying, ﴿And exalted is Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾, it contains two benefits:

One of them: that He, glorified is He, declared Himself free from what is unfitting for Him in His essence and wisdom, so that this would be a preface to the validity of Moses' prophethood, peace be upon him.

The second: that this may be a notification that this matter is willed by Him and brought into being by the Lord of the worlds, as an alert that what occurs is among the great affairs and the momentous events.

As for His saying, ﴿Indeed, it is I, Allah, the Exalted in Might, the Wise﴾, the author of al-Kashshaf said: the pronoun in ﴿innahu﴾ may be the pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-shaʾn), and ﴿Anā Allāh﴾ is a subject and predicate, and ﴿the Exalted in Might, the Wise﴾ are two qualifiers of the predicate. It may also refer back to what the preceding words indicate, meaning: your Speaker is "I", and "Allah" is an explanation of "I", and "the Exalted in Might, the Wise" are two qualifiers used for identification. This is a preface to the miracle which He intended to manifest through his hand. The meaning is: I am the Strong, the Capable of what is far from imagination, such as turning the staff into a serpent, the Doer of what I do with wisdom and planning. If it is said: this call could be from someone other than Allah, the Exalted, so how did Moses, peace be upon him, know that it was from Allah? The answer: the People of the Sunnah have two methods regarding this:

The first: that he heard speech which is free from resemblance to letters and sounds, so he knew by necessity that it is an attribute of Allah, the Exalted.

The second: the saying of the imams of Transoxiana (ma warāʾ al-nahr), namely that he, peace be upon him, heard the voice from the tree. We say: he knew that this was from Allah, the Exalted, for several reasons:

One of them: that when a call occurs from the fire or the tree, it is known that it is from Allah, the Exalted, because none of us is able to do that. This is weak, because it is possible to say: a devil entered the fire and the tree and then called out.

The second: it is possible that the call itself reached such magnitude that it could only be a miracle. This too is weak, because we do not know the measures of the powers of the angels and the devils, so there is no limit beyond which their doing it is impossible.

The third: that it was accompanied by a miracle which indicated that, so it was said: the fire was blazing in a green tree and did not burn it, and this became like a miracle. This is the most correct, and Allah knows best.

The fifth: the saying of the author of al-Kashshaf: ﴿Blessed is whoever is in the fire﴾, i.e., whoever is in the place of the fire, and whoever is around the place of it, which is the blessed spot mentioned in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿from the right side of the valley, in the blessed spot﴾ [al-Qasas: 30]. Evidence for this is the reading of Ubayy: "Blessed be the earth and whoever is around it," and also from him: "Blessed be the fire."

The third discussion: the reason for which the spot was blessed, and whoever is in it and around it was blessed, is the occurrence in it of this great matter, which is Allah's speaking to Moses, peace be upon him, and His appointing him as a messenger and manifesting miracles upon him. For this reason Allah made the land of Syria marked with blessings, in His saying: ﴿And We delivered him and Lot to the land which We have blessed for the worlds﴾ [al-Anbiya: 71]. It was fitting that it should be so, for it is the place where the prophets, may the blessings of Allah be upon them, were sent, the descent place of revelation, and their gathering place, whether living or dead.

The fourth discussion: that He, glorified is He, made this speech a preface to Moses' intimate conversation (munajah), peace be upon him. So His saying, ﴿Blessed is whoever is in the fire and whoever is around it﴾, indicates that a great matter has been decreed, from which blessing spreads throughout the entire land of Syria. As for His saying, ﴿And exalted is Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾, it contains two benefits:

One of them: that He, glorified is He, declared Himself free from what is unfitting for Him in His essence and wisdom, so that this would be a preface to the validity of Moses' prophethood, peace be upon him.

The second: that this may be a notification that this matter is willed by Him and brought into being by the Lord of the worlds, as an alert that what occurs is among the great affairs and the momentous events.

As for His saying, ﴿Indeed, it is I, Allah, the Exalted in Might, the Wise﴾, the author of al-Kashshaf said: the pronoun in ﴿innahu﴾ may be the pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-shaʾn), and ﴿Anā Allāh﴾ is a subject and predicate, and ﴿the Exalted in Might, the Wise﴾ are two qualifiers of the predicate. It may also refer back to what the preceding words indicate, meaning: your Speaker is "I", and "Allah" is an explanation of "I", and "the Exalted in Might, the Wise" are two qualifiers used for identification. This is a preface to the miracle which He intended to manifest through his hand. The meaning is: I am the Strong, the Capable of what is far from imagination, such as turning the staff into a serpent, the Doer of what I do with wisdom and planning. If it is said: this call could be from someone other than Allah, the Exalted, so how did Moses, peace be upon him, know that it was from Allah? The answer: the People of the Sunnah have two methods regarding this:

The first: that he heard speech which is free from resemblance to letters and sounds, so he knew by necessity that it is an attribute of Allah, the Exalted.

The second: the saying of the imams of Transoxiana (ma warāʾ al-nahr), namely that he, peace be upon him, heard the voice from the tree. We say: he knew that this was from Allah, the Exalted, for several reasons:

One of them: that when a call occurs from the fire or the tree, it is known that it is from Allah, the Exalted, because none of us is able to do that. This is weak, because it is possible to say: a devil entered the fire and the tree and then called out.

The second: it is possible that the call itself reached such magnitude that it could only be a miracle. This too is weak, because we do not know the measures of the powers of the angels and the devils, so there is no limit beyond which their doing it is impossible.

The third: that it was accompanied by a miracle which indicated that, so it was said: the fire was blazing in a green tree and did not burn it, and this became like a miracle. This is the most correct, and Allah knows best.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 27, verses 6–9:**

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And indeed, you are receiving the Qur'an from the Wise, the All-Knowing.﴾ ﴿When Moses said to his family, "Indeed, I have perceived a fire. I will bring you from it some news, or bring you a burning brand that you may warm yourselves."﴾ ﴿But when he came to it, he was called, "Blessed is whoever is in the fire and whoever is around it. And exalted is Allah, Lord of the worlds."﴾ ﴿"O Moses, indeed it is I, Allah, the Exalted in Might, the Wise."﴾

As for His saying, ﴿And indeed, you are receiving the Qur'an from the Wise, the All-Knowing﴾, its meaning is: you are being given it and receiving it from the presence of a Wise One and an All-Knowing One. This is the meaning of their coming in indefinite form (nakiratayn). This verse is a foundation and a preface for the stories that He wishes to relate after it. The word ﴿idh﴾ ("when") is in the accusative case, governed by an implied verb, which is "remember" (udhkur). It is as if He said: "Following that, take the story of Moses as one of the traces of His wisdom and knowledge." It is also permissible for it to be governed by "All-Knowing" (ʿalim). If it is asked: "Wisdom is either the same as knowledge, and knowledge is either included within it. Since He mentioned wisdom, why did He mention knowledge?" The answer: wisdom is knowledge of practical matters only, and knowledge is more general than it, because knowledge may be practical and may be theoretical, and theoretical sciences are more noble than practical sciences. So He mentioned wisdom, which includes the practical sciences, then mentioned "the All-Knowing" (al-ʿAlim), who is one who has attained perfection in knowledge. Perfection of knowledge is attained from three aspects: its unity, the comprehensiveness of its relation to all known things, and its remaining preserved from all changes. These three perfections are found only in the knowledge of Him, glorified and exalted is He.

Know that Allah, the Exalted, mentioned in this surah several kinds of stories.

The first story: the story of Moses, peace be upon him.

As for His saying, ﴿When Moses said to his family﴾, it indicates that with Moses, peace be upon him, there was no one except his wife, the daughter of Shuʿayb, peace be upon him. Allah, the Exalted, referred to her by the term "family" (ahl), and what follows this is the address being in the plural form, which is His saying ﴿Stay﴾ (imkthu).

As for His saying, ﴿Indeed, I have perceived a fire﴾, the meaning is that the two of them were travelling at night, the path had become confused for them, and it was a time of cold. In such a situation the soul is comforted by seeing a fire from a distance, because there is hope in it of removing the confusion about the path and of benefiting from the fire for warming oneself (iṣṭilaʾ). Therefore he gave them good news, saying: ﴿Indeed, I have perceived a fire﴾. The scholars differed. Some said: the intended meaning is "I saw and beheld." Others said: rather, the intended meaning is "I encountered and found, and so I was comforted by it." The first is closer, because they do not distinguish between the speaker's saying "I was comforted by my sight" and "I saw with my sight."

As for His saying, ﴿I will bring you from it some news﴾, "news" (khabar) is that which is reported about the state of the path, because he had gone astray. Then there is an omission in the speech, which is that when he saw the fire he headed towards it and said: ﴿I will bring you from it some news﴾, by which he would know the path.

As for His saying, ﴿or bring you a burning brand (shihab qabas)﴾, "shihab" is a flame, and "qabas" is a fire taken from another fire. He attributed "shihab" to "qabas" because it may be a qabas or not a qabas. Whoever reads it with tanwin (nunation) makes "qabas" a substitute (badal) or a qualifier for what is in it of the meaning of "qabas". Then here there are questions:

The first question: ﴿I will bring you from it some news﴾ and ﴿Perhaps I will bring you from it some news﴾ seem to contradict each other, because one indicates hope and the other certainty. We say: its answer is that the one who hopes, when his hope is strong, may say "I will do such-and-such and it will be such-and-such" while allowing for the possibility of failure.

The second question: why did he use the future particle of postponement (sin al-tasweef)? The answer: it is a promise from him to his family that he will bring it to them, even if he is slow or the distance is great.

The third question: why did he put "or" (aw) between the two matters, and why did he not combine them, since he needed both together? The answer: he based his hope on the fact that if he did not obtain these two aims, he would obtain one of them: either guidance to the path, or taking a fire-brand, trusting in the custom of Allah, the Exalted, because He hardly combines two deprivations upon His servant.

* * *

As for His saying, the Exalted, ﴿so that you may warm yourselves﴾, the meaning is "in order that you may warm yourselves." This indicates that they had a need for warming themselves, and in that case this can only be in a time of cold.

**The First Story: The Story of Moses (peace be upon him)**

﴿Cast down your staff.' And when he saw it moving as if it were a snake, he turned back in retreat and did not return. 'O Moses, do not fear. Indeed, the messengers do not fear in My presence. Except one who wrongs and then substitutes good after evil; indeed, I am Forgiving and Merciful. His statement, may He be exalted:

[Page 158]
﴿Cast down your staff. And when he saw it moving as if it were a snake, he turned back in retreat and did not return. O Moses, do not fear. Indeed, the messengers do not fear in My presence. Except one who wrongs and then substitutes good after evil; indeed, I am Forgiving and Merciful. And insert your hand into your pocket; it will come out white without disease, among nine signs to Pharaoh and his people. Indeed, they have been a defiantly disobedient people. And when Our signs came to them, visible, they said, "This is clear magic." And they denied them, though their souls were convinced of them, out of injustice and arrogance. So observe how was the end of the corrupters.﴾? Know that most of what is in these verses has already been explained, but let us mention what is specific to this passage. It is asked: to what did His statement ﴿Cast down your staff﴾ get conjoined? Its answer: it is conjoined to "Blessed is" (بُورِكَ), because the meaning is: "It was called out: blessed is whoever is in the fire, and: cast down your staff." Both are an explanation of "it was called out" (نُودِيَ).

As for His statement ﴿as if it were a snake (جانٌّ)﴾: the jann is a small snake. It was named jann because it hides (يَسْتَتِرُ) from people. Al-Hasan read "jānnun" (with a nominative ending) according to the dialect of those who avoid the meeting of two unvocalized consonants, so they say shābbah and dābbah.

As for His statement ﴿and he did not return (لَمْ يُعَقِّبْ)﴾: its meaning is that he did not come back. It is said: "the fighter 'aqqaba" when he passes by again after fleeing. He feared only because he thought that it was for a matter intended against him, and His statement ﴿Indeed, the messengers do not fear in My presence﴾ indicates this. Some said: the meaning is that when I command them to display a miracle, they should not fear regarding the display of that; otherwise, a sender (of messengers) may certainly fear.

As for His statement, may He be exalted, ﴿Except one who wrongs﴾: its meaning is "but one who has been wronged." It is to be understood as referring to what issues from the prophets, such as abandoning the better course or a minor sin. It is also possible that the intended meaning is an allusion to what occurred from Moses, which is one of the subtle allusions. Al-Hasan, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "By Allah, Moses was among those who wronged by killing the Copt, then he substituted (good for evil). For he (peace be upon him) said: ﴿My Lord, I have wronged myself, so forgive me﴾ [al-Qasas: 16]." It was also recited as "Alā man ẓalama" with the particle of alerting.

As for His statement, may He be exalted, ﴿then substituted good after evil﴾: what is meant is the goodness of repentance and the evil of sin. From Abu Bakr, in the transmission of ʿĀṣim, the reading is "ḥasanan."

As for His statement ﴿among nine signs﴾: it is a new (independent) sentence, and the preposition in it is connected to an omitted verb, and the meaning is: "Go with nine signs to Pharaoh." Someone may say: the signs were eleven, two of which are the hand and the staff, and the nine are: the splitting (of the sea), the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs, the blood, the obliteration (of their wealth), the drought in their deserts, and the shortage in their fields.

As for His statement ﴿When Our signs came to them, visible﴾: He attributed seeing (إبصار) to them, though in reality it belongs to the one who reflects upon them, and that is because of their looking at them and contemplating them. Or they are described as though, because of their clarity, they "see" and thereby guide. ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn and Qatāda read "mabṣara" (a place of seeing), which is like "majbana" (a place of cowardice) and "mabkhala" (a place of stinginess), meaning a place where there is much seeing.

As for His statement ﴿though their souls were convinced of them﴾: the waw in it is the waw of the circumstantial clause, and after it there is an implied verb. The benefit of mentioning "souls" is that they denied them with their tongues while being certain of them in their hearts and consciences. And "istiyqān" (certainty) is more emphatic than "iyqān" (conviction).

As for His statement ﴿out of injustice and arrogance﴾: what injustice is more grievous than the injustice of one who is certain that they are clear signs from Allah, may He be exalted, and then obstinately names them clear magic? As for arrogance, it is pride and disdain toward belief in what Moses brought, like His statement: ﴿So they were arrogant, and they were a haughty people﴾ [al-Muʾminun: 46]. It was also recited as "ʿulīyan" and "ʿilīyan," with a damma and with a kasra, just as "ʿitīyan" was recited. And Allah knows best.

**The Second Story: The Story of David and Solomon (peace be upon them both)**

﴿And We certainly gave David and Solomon knowledge. And they said, "Praise be to Allah, who has favored us over many of His believing servants."﴾ [Page 159]
﴿And Solomon inherited from David. And he said, "O people, we have been taught the speech of birds, and we have been given of all things. Indeed, this is the clear favor."﴾ ﴿And gathered for Solomon were his soldiers of the jinn and mankind and the birds, and they were marshaled in order.﴾ ﴿Until, when they came upon the valley of the ants, an ant said, "O ants, enter your dwellings lest Solomon and his soldiers crush you while they do not perceive."﴾ ﴿So he smiled, laughing at her words, and said, "My Lord, enable me to be grateful for Your favor which You have bestowed upon me and upon my parents, and to do righteousness that pleases You. And admit me by Your mercy among Your righteous servants."﴾

His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿And We certainly gave David and Solomon knowledge. And they said, "Praise be to Allah, who has favored us over many of His believing servants."﴾ ﴿And Solomon inherited from David. And he said, "O people, we have been taught the speech of birds, and we have been given of all things. Indeed, this is the clear favor."﴾ ﴿And gathered for Solomon were his soldiers of the jinn and mankind and the birds, and they were marshaled in order.﴾ ﴿Until, when they came upon the valley of the ants, an ant said, "O ants, enter your dwellings lest Solomon and his soldiers crush you while they do not perceive."﴾ ﴿So he smiled, laughing at her words, and said, "My Lord, enable me to be grateful for Your favor which You have bestowed upon me and upon my parents, and to do righteousness that pleases You. And admit me by Your mercy among Your righteous servants."﴾.

As for His statement, may He be exalted, ﴿knowledge (ʿilman)﴾: what is meant is a portion of knowledge, or a lofty and abundant knowledge. If it is asked: is this not the place for "fa" rather than "waw," like your saying, "I gave him and he thanked"? Its answer: thanking with the tongue is only fitting when it is preceded by the action of the heart, which is the resolve to perform obedience and abandon disobedience, and by the action of the limbs, which is occupation with acts of obedience. Since thanking with the tongue must be preceded by both, it is as if He had said: "We gave them both knowledge, so they acted upon it with heart and body, and they said with the tongue: 'Praise be to Allah, who did such and such.'"

* * *

As for His statement, may He be exalted, ﴿Praise be to Allah, who has favored us over many of His believing servants﴾, there are several points concerning it:

First: the "many" who were favored over are those who were not given knowledge, or who were not given the like of their knowledge. And in it is that they were favored over many, and many were favored over them.

Second: the verse indicates the high rank of knowledge, because they were given a kingdom that no one else was given, yet their thanks for knowledge was not like their thanks for the kingdom.

Third: they did not prefer themselves over everyone, and this indicates the goodness of humility.

Fourth: the apparent meaning requires that this favor is none other than that knowledge. Then knowledge of Allah and His attributes is nobler than other knowledge, so it is necessary that this thanks be only for this knowledge. Moreover, this knowledge is attained by all believers, so it is impossible that it be the cause of their favor over (other) believers. Therefore it must be that knowledge of Allah and His attributes becomes so clear that a person is absorbed in it, such that no doubts come to mind and the heart never neglects it at any time or at any moment.

* * *

[Page 160]
As for His statement, may He be exalted, ﴿And Solomon inherited from David﴾, they have disagreed about it. Al-Hasan said: it is wealth, because prophethood is an originating gift and is not inherited. Others said: rather it is prophethood. And others said: rather it is kingship and governance. If al-Hasan had reflected, he would have known that when a child inherits wealth, it too is an originating gift from Allah, may He be exalted. That is why a child inherits if he is a believer and does not inherit if he is a disbeliever or a killer. But Allah, may He be exalted, made the cause of inheritance for the one who inherits to be death, subject to conditions. Prophethood is not like that, because death is not a cause for a son's prophethood. So in this respect they differ. And that does not prevent saying that he inherited prophethood, since he took it up upon the death (of his father), just as a child inherits wealth when he takes it up upon the death (of his father). Among what clarifies what we have said is that if He had specified and said, "And Solomon inherited from David his wealth," then His statement "And he said, 'O people, we have been taught the speech of birds'" would have no meaning. But when we say "and inherited his station of prophethood and kingship," that is fitting, because learning the speech of birds falls within what he inherited. Similarly His statement, "and we have been given of all things," because the heir to kingship comprises that, whereas the heir to wealth does not. And His statement, "Indeed, this is the clear favor," also suits only what we have mentioned and not wealth, which may be attained by both the perfect and the deficient. And what Allah, may He be exalted, mentions of Solomon's soldiers after him suits only what we have mentioned. So by what we have mentioned, the view of those who claim he inherited only wealth is refuted. As for saying that he inherited wealth and kingship together, this is not refuted by the aspects we have mentioned, but by the apparent meaning of his (peace be upon him) saying: "We, the company of prophets, do not leave inheritance."

As for His statement, ﴿O people﴾: what is meant by it is to publicize Allah's favor, to honor it, and to call people to believe by means of the mention of the miracle, which is knowledge of the speech of birds. The author of al-Kashshaf said: "Manṭiq (speech) is everything that is vocalized, whether single or compound, meaningful or meaningless. Yaʿqūb titled his book 'Iṣlāḥ al-Manṭiq' and he corrected in it only single words. The Arabs also say: 'the dove spoke (nataqat al-ḥamāma).'" So what Solomon (peace be upon him) was taught of the speech of birds is what some of them understand from others of their intentions and purposes.

As for His statement, may He be exalted, ﴿and we have been given of all things﴾: what is meant is the abundance of what was given, because the whole and a large part share the attribute of abundance, and sharing is a basis for permitting metaphor. Therefore the word "all" is used for "much." A similar example is His statement: ﴿and she was given of all things﴾.

As for His statement, ﴿Indeed, this is the clear favor﴾: it is an affirmation of His statement, ﴿Praise be to Allah, who has favored us﴾, and what is intended by it is thanks and praise, as he (peace be upon him) said: "I am the master of the children of Adam, and I say this without boasting." If it is asked: how did he say "we have been taught" and "we have been given," when that is the speech of the arrogant? Its answer is in two respects:

The first: he intends himself and his father.

The second: this "we" is called the "we" of the one who is obeyed, and he was an obeyed king. The interests of the people may depend on exalting the king, and so that exaltation becomes obligatory.

As for His statement ﴿as if it were a snake (جانٌّ)﴾: the jann is a small snake. It was named jann because it hides (يَسْتَتِرُ) from people. Al-Hasan read "jānnun" (with a nominative ending) according to the dialect of those who avoid the meeting of two unvocalized consonants, so they say shābbah and dābbah.

As for His statement ﴿and he did not return (لَمْ يُعَقِّبْ)﴾: its meaning is that he did not come back. It is said: "the fighter 'aqqaba" when he passes by again after fleeing. He feared only because he thought that it was for a matter intended against him, and His statement ﴿Indeed, the messengers do not fear in My presence﴾ indicates this. Some said: the meaning is that when I command them to display a miracle, they should not fear regarding the display of that; otherwise, a sender (of messengers) may certainly fear.

It is to be understood as referring to what issues from the prophets, such as abandoning the better course or a minor sin. It is also possible that the intended meaning is an allusion to what occurred from Moses, which is one of the subtle allusions. **The Second Story: The Story of David and Solomon (peace be upon them both)**

As for His statement, may He be exalted, ﴿knowledge (ʿilman)﴾: what is meant is a portion of knowledge, or a lofty and abundant knowledge. If it is asked: is this not the place for "fa" rather than "waw," like your saying, "I gave him and he thanked"? Its answer: thanking with the tongue is only fitting when it is preceded by the action of the heart, which is the resolve to perform obedience and abandon disobedience, and by the action of the limbs, which is occupation with acts of obedience. Since thanking with the tongue must be preceded by both, it is as if He had said: "We gave them both knowledge, so they acted upon it with heart and body, and they said with the tongue: 'Praise be to Allah, who did such and such.'"

* * *

As for His statement, may He be exalted, ﴿Praise be to Allah, who has favored us over many of His believing servants﴾, there are several points concerning it:

First: the "many" who were favored over are those who were not given knowledge, or who were not given the like of their knowledge. And in it is that they were favored over many, and many were favored over them.

Second: the verse indicates the high rank of knowledge, because they were given a kingdom that no one else was given, yet their thanks for knowledge was not like their thanks for the kingdom.

Third: they did not prefer themselves over everyone, and this indicates the goodness of humility.

Fourth: the apparent meaning requires that this favor is none other than that knowledge. Then knowledge of Allah and His attributes is nobler than other knowledge, so it is necessary that this thanks be only for this knowledge. Moreover, this knowledge is attained by all believers, so it is impossible that it be the cause of their favor over (other) believers. Therefore it must be that knowledge of Allah and His attributes becomes so clear that a person is absorbed in it, such that no doubts come to mind and the heart never neglects it at any time or at any moment.

[Page 160]
As for His statement, may He be exalted, ﴿And Solomon inherited from David﴾, they have disagreed about it. Al-Hasan said: it is wealth, because prophethood is an originating gift and is not inherited. Others said: rather it is prophethood. And others said: rather it is kingship and governance. If al-Hasan had reflected, he would have known that when a child inherits wealth, it too is an originating gift from Allah, may He be exalted. That is why a child inherits if he is a believer and does not inherit if he is a disbeliever or a killer. But Allah, may He be exalted, made the cause of inheritance for the one who inherits to be death, subject to conditions. Prophethood is not like that, because death is not a cause for a son's prophethood. So in this respect they differ. And that does not prevent saying that he inherited prophethood, since he took it up upon the death (of his father), just as a child inherits wealth when he takes it up upon the death (of his father). But when we say "and inherited his station of prophethood and kingship," that is fitting, because learning the speech of birds falls within what he inherited. Similarly His statement, "and we have been given of all things," because the heir to kingship comprises that, whereas the heir to wealth does not. And His statement, "Indeed, this is the clear favor," also suits only what we have mentioned and not wealth, which may be attained by both the perfect and the deficient. And what Allah, may He be exalted, mentions of Solomon's soldiers after him suits only what we have mentioned. So by what we have mentioned, the view of those who claim he inherited only wealth is refuted. As for saying that he inherited wealth and kingship together, this is not refuted by the aspects we have mentioned, but by the apparent meaning of his (peace be upon him) saying: "We, the company of prophets, do not leave inheritance."

[Page 160]
As for His statement, may He be exalted, ﴿And Solomon inherited from David﴾, they have disagreed about it. As for His statement, ﴿Indeed, this is the clear favor﴾: it is an affirmation of His statement, ﴿Praise be to Allah, who has favored us﴾, and what is intended by it is thanks and praise, as he (peace be upon him) said: "I am the master of the children of Adam, and I say this without boasting." **The First Story: The Story of Moses (peace be upon him)**

﴿Cast down your staff.' And when he saw it moving as if it were a snake, he turned back in retreat and did not return. 'O Moses, do not fear. Indeed, the messengers do not fear in My presence. Except one who wrongs and then substitutes good after evil; indeed, I am Forgiving and Merciful. So observe how was the end of the corrupters.﴾

His statement, may He be exalted:

[Page 158]
﴿Cast down your staff. And when he saw it moving as if it were a snake, he turned back in retreat and did not return. O Moses, do not fear. Indeed, the messengers do not fear in My presence. Except one who wrongs and then substitutes good after evil; indeed, I am Forgiving and Merciful. And insert your hand into your pocket; it will come out white without disease, among nine signs to Pharaoh and his people. Indeed, they have been a defiantly disobedient people. And when Our signs came to them, visible, they said, "This is clear magic." And they denied them, though their souls were convinced of them, out of injustice and arrogance. So observe how was the end of the corrupters.﴾? Know that most of what is in these verses has already been explained, but let us mention what is specific to this passage. It is asked: to what did His statement ﴿Cast down your staff﴾ get conjoined? Its answer: it is conjoined to "Blessed is" (بُورِكَ), because the meaning is: "It was called out: blessed is whoever is in the fire, and: cast down your staff." Both are an explanation of "it was called out" (نُودِيَ).

As for His statement ﴿as if it were a snake (جانٌّ)﴾: the jann is a small snake. It was named jann because it hides (يَسْتَتِرُ) from people. Al-Hasan read "jānnun" (with a nominative ending) according to the dialect of those who avoid the meeting of two unvocalized consonants, so they say shābbah and dābbah.

As for His statement ﴿and he did not return (لَمْ يُعَقِّبْ)﴾: its meaning is that he did not come back. It is said: "the fighter 'aqqaba" when he passes by again after fleeing. He feared only because he thought that it was for a matter intended against him, and His statement ﴿Indeed, the messengers do not fear in My presence﴾ indicates this. Some said: the meaning is that when I command them to display a miracle, they should not fear regarding the display of that; otherwise, a sender (of messengers) may certainly fear.

As for His statement, may He be exalted, ﴿Except one who wrongs﴾: its meaning is "but one who has been wronged." It is to be understood as referring to what issues from the prophets, such as abandoning the better course or a minor sin. It is also possible that the intended meaning is an allusion to what occurred from Moses, which is one of the subtle allusions. Al-Hasan, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "By Allah, Moses was among those who wronged by killing the Copt, then he substituted (good for evil). For he (peace be upon him) said: ﴿My Lord, I have wronged myself, so forgive me﴾ [al-Qasas: 16]." It was also recited as "Alā man ẓalama" with the particle of alerting.

As for His statement, may He be exalted, ﴿then substituted good after evil﴾: what is meant is the goodness of repentance and the evil of sin. From Abu Bakr, in the transmission of ʿĀṣim, the reading is "ḥasanan."

As for His statement ﴿among nine signs﴾: it is a new (independent) sentence, and the preposition in it is connected to an omitted verb, and the meaning is: "Go with nine signs to Pharaoh." Someone may say: the signs were eleven, two of which are the hand and the staff, and the nine are: the splitting (of the sea), the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs, the blood, the obliteration (of their wealth), the drought in their deserts, and the shortage in their fields.

As for His statement ﴿When Our signs came to them, visible﴾: He attributed seeing (إبصار) to them, though in reality it belongs to the one who reflects upon them, and that is because of their looking at them and contemplating them. Or they are described as though, because of their clarity, they "see" and thereby guide. ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn and Qatāda read "mabṣara" (a place of seeing), which is like "majbana" (a place of cowardice) and "mabkhala" (a place of stinginess), meaning a place where there is much seeing.

As for His statement ﴿though their souls were convinced of them﴾: the waw in it is the waw of the circumstantial clause, and after it there is an implied verb. The benefit of mentioning "souls" is that they denied them with their tongues while being certain of them in their hearts and consciences. And "istiyqān" (certainty) is more emphatic than "iyqān" (conviction).

As for His statement ﴿out of injustice and arrogance﴾: what injustice is more grievous than the injustice of one who is certain that they are clear signs from Allah, may He be exalted, and then obstinately names them clear magic? As for arrogance, it is pride and disdain toward belief in what Moses brought, like His statement: ﴿So they were arrogant, and they were a haughty people﴾ [al-Muʾminun: 46]. It was also recited as "ʿulīyan" and "ʿilīyan," with a damma and with a kasra, just as "ʿitīyan" was recited. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (*Mafatih al-Ghayb*) on Surah 27, verses 17–19:

As for His saying, ﴿And for Solomon were gathered his armies of the jinn and mankind and birds﴾, *al-hashr* means bringing together and assembling from different places. The meaning is that God, exalted is He, made all these kinds his armies. This cannot be so unless they are directed according to his will. It also cannot be so except with intellect, which makes obligation (*taklif*) valid, or they must be like an adolescent who has nearly reached the age of obligation. Therefore we say that God, exalted is He, gave the birds in his time something of intellect. This is not the state of birds in our time, although some of them have been granted by God the subtleties for which they are needed, or which God has given them for the benefit of people, like the bee and others.

[p. 161]

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿so they are held back﴾, its meaning is that they are restrained. This can only be if each group among them has a *wazi'* (an overseer), who has authority over whoever turns back, holds back, or diverts them. The apparent meaning supports this much. What is reported in the *khabar* (report), that they used to prevent anyone from advancing so that his march with his armies would be in order, is not impossible.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿until, when they came upon the valley of the ants﴾, it is said that it was a valley in Syria with many ants. It may be asked: why was *atau* (came upon) followed by *'ala* (upon)? The answer is in two ways:

The first: their coming was from above, so the preposition of elevation (*'ala*) was used.

The second: it may mean crossing the valley and reaching its end, from the expression *ata 'ala al-shay'* when one reaches its end, as if they intended to descend at the end of the valley. It was also read as *namulatun ya ayyuha al-numul* with a *damma* on the *mim* and on the *nun* and *mim*. The original form was *al-namul*, on the pattern of *al-rajul*, and the *namul* that is in common use is a lightened form of it.

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿aninth of the ants said﴾, the meaning is that she spoke these words. This is not improbable, for God, exalted is He, is able to create in her intellect and speech. It is reported from Qatadah that he entered Kufa, and people crowded around him, and he said: "Ask me about whatever you wish." Abu Hanifa, may God have mercy on him, was present, and he was a young man. He said: "Ask him about the ant of Solomon: was she male or female?" They asked him, and he was silenced. Abu Hanifa, may God be pleased with him, said: "She was female." It was said to him: "How do you know?" He said: "From the Book of God, exalted is He, which is His saying: ﴿aninth of the ants said﴾. Had she been male, it would have said *qala namlatun* (a male form of the verb). This is because *namlah* is like *hamamah* (dove) and *shah* (sheep) in applying to both male and female, so they are distinguished by a sign, as in the phrases *hamamah dhakar* (male dove) and *hamamah unthā* (female dove), and *huwa* and *hiya*."

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Enter your dwellings﴾, know that when the ant had nearly reached the limit of intellect, she was therefore addressed in the way rational beings are addressed. This is why God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Enter your dwellings﴾. If you ask, "What is ﴿lest they crush you﴾?" I say: it may be a reply to the command, or it may be a prohibition in place of the command. The meaning is: do not remain where you are, lest he crush you, in the manner of *la arayannaka hahuna* (I will not see you here).

In this verse there are several points of instruction:

The first: whoever walks along the road is not obliged to take precautions; rather, it is those who are on the road who must take precautions.

The second: the ant said, ﴿while they do not perceive﴾, as if she knew that the prophet is protected from sin, so that killing these creatures would only happen by way of forgetfulness. This is a great indication of the obligation to affirm firmly the infallibility (*'ismah*) of the prophets, peace be upon them.

The third: I saw in some books that this ant only ordered the others to enter because she feared for her people that, if they saw Solomon in his majesty, they might fall into ingratitude for God's blessing. This is what is meant by His saying, ﴿lest Solomon and his armies crush you﴾. So she ordered them to enter their dwellings so that they would not see those blessings and would not fall into ingratitude for God's blessing. This is an indication that sitting with the people of worldly status is to be avoided.

The fourth: it was read as *maskanakum* and *la yahtimannakum* with the *nun* lightened, and it was read as *la yahtamannakum* with the *ta'* having a *fatha* and a *kasra*. Its original form is *yahtimannakum*.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿So he smiled, laughing, at her words﴾, it means he smiled and began to laugh, meaning that he went beyond the limit of smiling to laughing. He laughed for two reasons:

One of them: his admiration for what her words indicated of the manifestation of his mercy and the mercy of his armies, and of the renown of his state and theirs in the matter of piety. This is her saying: ﴿while they do not perceive﴾.

The second: his joy at what God had given him, which He had not given anyone else, in hearing the speech of the ant and comprehending its meaning.

[p. 162]

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿My Lord, enable me﴾, the author of *al-Kashshaf* said: The real meaning of *awzi'ni* is: make me hold to the thanks for Your blessing that is with me, and restrain it from turning away from me, until I am always grateful to You. This indicates our doctrine, for according to the Mu'tazilah, whatever favors (*alutf*) it is possible to do have been done, and seeking the attainment of what is already attained is futile.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and upon my parents﴾, this is because he counted God's blessings upon his parents as a blessing upon himself. The meaning of His saying, ﴿and that I may do righteousness that You will accept﴾, is seeking help in gratitude and in righteous deeds. Then He said: ﴿and admit me by Your mercy among Your righteous servants.﴾ Since he asked for help in the world for good deeds, he asked to be placed among the righteous in the Hereafter. His saying, ﴿by Your mercy﴾, indicates that entering Paradise is by His mercy and grace, not by any merit on the part of the servant. Know that Solomon, peace be upon him, asked first for what would be a means to the reward of the Hereafter, and then asked for the reward of the Hereafter itself. As for the means to reward, it consists of two matters:

One of them: thanking for the previous blessing.

The second: occupying oneself with all kinds of service.

As for occupying oneself with thanking for the previous blessing, it is His saying, exalted is He, ﴿My Lord, enable me to be grateful for Your favor which You have bestowed upon me﴾. Since the bestowal of blessing upon the fathers is a bestowal upon the sons, because a son's descent from a noble father is a blessing from God upon the son, he therefore occupied himself with thanking God for His blessings upon the fathers by saying: ﴿and upon my parents﴾. As for occupying oneself with all kinds of service, it is His saying: ﴿and that I may do righteousness that You will accept﴾. As for seeking the reward of the Hereafter, it is His saying: ﴿and admit me by Your mercy among Your righteous servants.﴾ If it is said: the ranks of the prophets are greater than the ranks of the saints and the righteous, so what is the reason that the prophets ask to be made among the righteous? Joseph said: ﴿Cause me to die as a Muslim and join me with the righteous﴾ [Yusuf 12:101], and Solomon said: ﴿and admit me by Your mercy among Your righteous servants﴾? The answer: the perfectly righteous is the one who does not disobey God, exalted is He, and does not intend to disobey. This is a lofty rank. And God knows best.

* * *

* * *

Then He said: ﴿and admit me by Your mercy among Your righteous servants.﴾ Since he asked for help in the world for good deeds, he asked to be placed among the righteous in the Hereafter. One of them: thanking for the previous blessing.

The second: occupying oneself with all kinds of service.

The meaning is that God, exalted is He, made all these kinds his armies. This cannot be so unless they are directed according to his will. It also cannot be so except with intellect, which makes obligation (*taklif*) valid, or they must be like an adolescent who has nearly reached the age of obligation. Therefore we say that God, exalted is He, gave the birds in his time something of intellect. This is not the state of birds in our time, although some of them have been granted by God the subtleties for which they are needed, or which God has given them for the benefit of people, like the bee and others.

[p. 161]

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿so they are held back﴾, its meaning is that they are restrained. This can only be if each group among them has a *wazi'* (an overseer), who has authority over whoever turns back, holds back, or diverts them. The apparent meaning supports this much. What is reported in the *khabar* (report), that they used to prevent anyone from advancing so that his march with his armies would be in order, is not impossible.

* * *

The first: their coming was from above, so the preposition of elevation (*'ala*) was used.

The second: it may mean crossing the valley and reaching its end, from the expression *ata 'ala al-shay'* when one reaches its end, as if they intended to descend at the end of the valley. It was also read as *namulatun ya ayyuha al-numul* with a *damma* on the *mim* and on the *nun* and *mim*. The original form was *al-namul*, on the pattern of *al-rajul*, and the *namul* that is in common use is a lightened form of it.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 27, verses 20–24:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And he inspected the birds and said, "Why do I not see the hoopoe? Or is he among the absent?"﴾ ﴿"I will surely punish him with a severe punishment, or slaughter him, or he must bring me a clear authority."﴾ ﴿But he remained not far off and said, "I have encompassed [knowledge of] what you have not encompassed, and I have come to you from Saba' with certain news."﴾ ﴿"Indeed, I found a woman ruling them, and she has been given of all things, and she has a great throne."﴾ ﴿"I found her and her people prostrating to the sun instead of Allah, and Satan has made their deeds appear fair to them and averted them from the way, so they are not guided."﴾

Know that when Sulayman, peace be upon him, inspected the birds, this implied that he inspected them for a matter specific to that bird. The scholars differed concerning the reason for which he inspected it, in several respects:

The first: the saying of Wahb, that it neglected the duty (nawba) it used to perform, and for this reason he inspected it.

The second: that he inspected it because the water-measuring instruments were in its care, and it knew the distinction between what is near and what is far; so, because Sulayman needed that, he sought it and inspected it.

The third: that it used to shade him from the sun, and when he lost that, he inspected it.

As for his saying, ﴿Why do I not see the hoopoe? Or is he among the absent?﴾: here "am" is the disjunctive (munqati'a). He looked at the place of the hoopoe and did not see it, so he said, "Why do I not see it?", meaning that he does not see it though it is present, due to a veil that concealed it or other than that. Then it occurred to him that it was absent, so he turned away from that and began to say, "Is it absent?" as if asking about the correctness of what had occurred to him. Similar to this is the saying of people: "Is it a camel or a sheep?"

As for his saying, ﴿I will surely punish him with a severe punishment, or slaughter him, or he must bring me a clear authority﴾: this is not permissible to say except regarding one who is accountable, or one who is close to reason so that he may be disciplined. Then they differed concerning his saying, ﴿I will surely punish him﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: it is plucking out the feathers and casting it into the sun. It was said: that it be smeared with tar and exposed to the sun. It was said: that it be thrown to ants so they eat it. It was said: placing it in a cage. It was said: separating it from its mate. It was said: "I will bind him to the company of opposites." And from some of them: "The narrowest of prisons is the company of opposites." It was said: "I will bind him to serving his peers."

As for his saying, ﴿But he remained﴾: it has been read with a fatha and a damma on the kaf. ﴿Not far off﴾ is like your saying "after a short while." He described his staying as brief in duration to indicate his hastening out of fear of Sulayman, and so that it would be known how the birds were subjugated to him.

As for his saying, ﴿I have encompassed [knowledge of] what you have not encompassed﴾: in it is an admonition to Sulayman that among the lowliest of Allah's creation there may be one who has encompassed knowledge of what he has not encompassed, so this is a gentle reminder against self-admiration. And "encompassing a thing in knowledge" means that it is known from all its aspects.

As for his saying, ﴿and I have come to you from Saba' with certain news﴾: know that Saba' has been read with tanwin and without it. It has also been transmitted with the ba' sukun. And from Ibn Kathir, in one narration, "Saba" with an alif, as in their saying "they went in the hands of Saba." He is Saba' ibn Yashjub ibn Ya'rub ibn Qahtan. Whoever makes it the name of a tribe does not apply tanwin; whoever makes it the name of a clan or the great forefather applies tanwin. Then the city of Ma'rib was named Saba', and between it and San'a' is a journey of three days. And "naba'" is news that has significance.

His saying, ﴿from Saba' with news﴾ is among the fine points of speech related to the wording, and the condition of its excellence is the soundness of its meaning. Here it has come exceeding mere soundness, so it is excellent in wording and meaning. Do you not see that if "bi-nabaʾ" were replaced with "bi-khabar," the meaning would still be sound, but the word naba' is more fitting because of the added significance that matches the description of the situation.

As for his saying, ﴿Indeed, I found a woman ruling them﴾: the woman is Bilqis daughter of Sharahil. Her father was king of the land of Yemen, and she and her people were Magians worshipping the sun. The pronoun in "ruling them" refers to Saba'. If by it is meant the people, the matter is clear; if the city is meant, the meaning is that she rules its inhabitants.

* * *

As for his saying, ﴿and she has been given of all things﴾: there is an objection here, namely how he said ﴿she has been given of all things﴾ while Sulayman said ﴿and we have been given of all things﴾, so it seems the hoopoe equated the two. The answer: Sulayman's saying refers to what he was given of prophethood and wisdom, then to kingship and the means of the world; but the hoopoe's saying refers only to what pertains to the world.

* * *

As for his saying, ﴿and she has a great throne﴾: there is an objection here, namely how the hoopoe considered her throne great while he saw the kingdom of Sulayman? Also, how did he equate the throne of Bilqis with the throne of Allah, exalted, in the description of greatness?

The answer to the first: it is possible that he regarded her condition as small in comparison to Sulayman's, and so he deemed that throne great for her; and it is possible that Sulayman, despite his grandeur, did not have one like it, as it may happen that some governors have something not like it in the sultan's possession.

As for the second: describing her throne as great is an exaltation of it relative to the thrones of the kings of her kind; and describing the throne of Allah as great is an exaltation of it in relation to all that He created of the heavens and the earth.

Know that there are two discussions here:

The first discussion: the heretics (malahida) attacked this story from several aspects:

The first: these verses include that the ant and the hoopoe spoke with a speech that only rational beings would produce, and this leads to sophistry. For if we permit that, we cannot be sure that the ant we observe in our time is not more knowledgeable in geometry than Euclid, and in grammar than Sibawayh; and likewise regarding the louse and the mite; and it is possible that among them are prophets, obligations, and miracles. And it is known that whoever permits that is closer to madness.

The second: Sulayman, peace be upon him, was in Syria, so how did the hoopoe fly in that delicate moment from Syria to Yemen and then return to him?

The third: how was the state of such a great queen hidden from Sulayman, peace be upon him, despite what is said: that the jinn and mankind were in obedience to Sulayman, and that he was the king of the whole world, and that she was under his banner, as it is said there were twelve thousand kings under the banner of each of whom were a hundred thousand; and despite what is said: that between Sulayman and the city of Bilqis, during the flight of the hoopoe, there was only a journey of three days.

The fourth: from where did the hoopoe acquire knowledge of Allah, exalted, the obligation of prostrating to Him, the denial of their prostration to the sun, its attribution to Satan, and its embellishment?

The answer to the first: that possibility exists at the outset of reason, and it is only removed by consensus (ijma'). As for the rest: belief in the world's need of a capable, choosing Creator removes these doubts.

The second discussion: the Mu'tazilah said: His saying, ﴿they prostrate to the sun instead of Allah, and Satan has made their deeds appear fair to them﴾ indicates that the act of the servant originates from him, because He, exalted, attributed it to Satan after attributing it to them; and because He placed it in the position of blame; and because He stated that they are not guided. The answer is in several aspects:

The first: this is the saying of the hoopoe, so it is not a proof.

The second: its apparent meaning is abandoned, for he said ﴿so he averted them from the way﴾, and according to them Satan does not avert the disbeliever from the way, since if he were barred and prevented, the obligation would fall from him. So there remains here only the reliance on the distinction of praise and blame. The answer has been given before on this point many times, so there is no benefit in repeating it. And Allah knows best.
