Or is he among the absent?"﴾ ﴿"I will surely punish him with a severe punishment, or slaughter him, or he must bring me a clear authority."﴾ ﴿But he remained not far off and said, "I have encompassed [knowledge of] what you have not encompassed, and I have come to you from Saba' with certain news."﴾ ﴿"Indeed, I found a woman ruling them, and she has been given of all things, and she has a great throne."﴾ ﴿"I found her and her people prostrating to the sun instead of Allah, and Satan has made their deeds appear fair to them and averted them from the way, so they are not guided."﴾

Know that when Sulayman, peace be upon him, inspected the birds, this implied that he inspected them for a matter specific to that bird. The scholars differed concerning the reason for which he inspected it, in several respects:

The first: the saying of Wahb, that it neglected the duty (nawba) it used to perform, and for this reason he inspected it.

The second: that he inspected it because the water-measuring instruments were in its care, and it knew the distinction between what is near and what is far; so, because Sulayman needed that, he sought it and inspected it.

The third: that it used to shade him from the sun, and when he lost that, he inspected it.

As for his saying, ﴿Why do I not see the hoopoe? Or is he among the absent?﴾: here "am" is the disjunctive (munqati'a). He looked at the place of the hoopoe and did not see it, so he said, "Why do I not see it?", meaning that he does not see it though it is present, due to a veil that concealed it or other than that. Then it occurred to him that it was absent, so he turned away from that and began to say, "Is it absent?" as if asking about the correctness of what had occurred to him. Similar to this is the saying of people: "Is it a camel or a sheep?"

As for his saying, ﴿I will surely punish him with a severe punishment, or slaughter him, or he must bring me a clear authority﴾: this is not permissible to say except regarding one who is accountable, or one who is close to reason so that he may be disciplined. Then they differed concerning his saying, ﴿I will surely punish him﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: it is plucking out the feathers and casting it into the sun. It was said: that it be smeared with tar and exposed to the sun. It was said: that it be thrown to ants so they eat it. It was said: placing it in a cage. It was said: separating it from its mate. It was said: "I will bind him to the company of opposites." And from some of them: "The narrowest of prisons is the company of opposites." It was said: "I will bind him to serving his peers."

As for his saying, ﴿But he remained﴾: it has been read with a fatha and a damma on the kaf. ﴿Not far off﴾ is like your saying "after a short while." He described his staying as brief in duration to indicate his hastening out of fear of Sulayman, and so that it would be known how the birds were subjugated to him.

As for his saying, ﴿I have encompassed [knowledge of] what you have not encompassed﴾: in it is an admonition to Sulayman that among the lowliest of Allah's creation there may be one who has encompassed knowledge of what he has not encompassed, so this is a gentle reminder against self-admiration. And "encompassing a thing in knowledge" means that it is known from all its aspects.

As for his saying, ﴿and I have come to you from Saba' with certain news﴾: know that Saba' has been read with tanwin and without it. It has also been transmitted with the ba' sukun. And from Ibn Kathir, in one narration, "Saba" with an alif, as in their saying "they went in the hands of Saba." He is Saba' ibn Yashjub ibn Ya'rub ibn Qahtan. Whoever makes it the name of a tribe does not apply tanwin; whoever makes it the name of a clan or the great forefather applies tanwin. Then the city of Ma'rib was named Saba', and between it and San'a' is a journey of three days. And "naba'" is news that has significance.

His saying, ﴿from Saba' with news﴾ is among the fine points of speech related to the wording, and the condition of its excellence is the soundness of its meaning. Here it has come exceeding mere soundness, so it is excellent in wording and meaning. Do you not see that if "bi-nabaʾ" were replaced with "bi-khabar," the meaning would still be sound, but the word naba' is more fitting because of the added significance that matches the description of the situation.

As for his saying, ﴿Indeed, I found a woman ruling them﴾: the woman is Bilqis daughter of Sharahil. Her father was king of the land of Yemen, and she and her people were Magians worshipping the sun. The pronoun in "ruling them" refers to Saba'. If by it is meant the people, the matter is clear; if the city is meant, the meaning is that she rules its inhabitants.

* * *

As for his saying, ﴿and she has been given of all things﴾: there is an objection here, namely how he said ﴿she has been given of all things﴾ while Sulayman said ﴿and we have been given of all things﴾, so it seems the hoopoe equated the two. The answer: Sulayman's saying refers to what he was given of prophethood and wisdom, then to kingship and the means of the world; but the hoopoe's saying refers only to what pertains to the world.

* * *

As for his saying, ﴿and she has a great throne﴾: there is an objection here, namely how the hoopoe considered her throne great while he saw the kingdom of Sulayman? Also, how did he equate the throne of Bilqis with the throne of Allah, exalted, in the description of greatness?

The answer to the first: it is possible that he regarded her condition as small in comparison to Sulayman's, and so he deemed that throne great for her; and it is possible that Sulayman, despite his grandeur, did not have one like it, as it may happen that some governors have something not like it in the sultan's possession.

As for the second: describing her throne as great is an exaltation of it relative to the thrones of the kings of her kind; and describing the throne of Allah as great is an exaltation of it in relation to all that He created of the heavens and the earth.

Know that there are two discussions here:

The first discussion: the heretics (malahida) attacked this story from several aspects:

The first: these verses include that the ant and the hoopoe spoke with a speech that only rational beings would produce, and this leads to sophistry. For if we permit that, we cannot be sure that the ant we observe in our time is not more knowledgeable in geometry than Euclid, and in grammar than Sibawayh; and likewise regarding the louse and the mite; and it is possible that among them are prophets, obligations, and miracles. And it is known that whoever permits that is closer to madness.

The second: Sulayman, peace be upon him, was in Syria, so how did the hoopoe fly in that delicate moment from Syria to Yemen and then return to him?

The third: how was the state of such a great queen hidden from Sulayman, peace be upon him, despite what is said: that the jinn and mankind were in obedience to Sulayman, and that he was the king of the whole world, and that she was under his banner, as it is said there were twelve thousand kings under the banner of each of whom were a hundred thousand; and despite what is said: that between Sulayman and the city of Bilqis, during the flight of the hoopoe, there was only a journey of three days.

The fourth: from where did the hoopoe acquire knowledge of Allah, exalted, the obligation of prostrating to Him, the denial of their prostration to the sun, its attribution to Satan, and its embellishment?

The answer to the first: that possibility exists at the outset of reason, and it is only removed by consensus (ijma'). As for the rest: belief in the world's need of a capable, choosing Creator removes these doubts.

The second discussion: the Mu'tazilah said: His saying, ﴿they prostrate to the sun instead of Allah, and Satan has made their deeds appear fair to them﴾ indicates that the act of the servant originates from him, because He, exalted, attributed it to Satan after attributing it to them; and because He placed it in the position of blame; and because He stated that they are not guided. The answer is in several aspects:

The first: this is the saying of the hoopoe, so it is not a proof.

The second: its apparent meaning is abandoned, for he said ﴿so he averted them from the way﴾, and according to them Satan does not avert the disbeliever from the way, since if he were barred and prevented, the obligation would fall from him. So there remains here only the reliance on the distinction of praise and blame. The answer has been given before on this point many times, so there is no benefit in repeating it. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 27, verses 25–28:

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿That they should not prostrate to Allah, who brings forth what is hidden in the heavens and the earth, and knows what you conceal and what you disclose.﴾ ﴿Allah—there is no deity except Him, Lord of the Mighty Throne.﴾ ﴿He said, "We will see whether you have told the truth or were among the liars."﴾ ﴿Go with this letter of mine and deliver it to them, then withdraw from them and see what they return.﴾

Regarding this there are several issues:

The first issue: Know that in His statement, exalted is He, ﴿Alla yasjudu﴾ (that they should not prostrate), there are several readings. The first is the reading of the one who reads with light stress, "alā" (ألا), where "alā" is for alerting (al-tanbīh) and "yā" is the particle of calling, and its object is omitted, as in the saying of the one who omitted it:

"Alā yā islamī yā dāra Mayya ʿalā al-bilā [wa lā zāla munhallan bi-jaraʿā-ki al-qaṭru]"
(Oh, may you be safe, O abode of Mayya, against decay, and may the rain never cease to pour upon your sandy hillocks.)

The second is with the emphatic stress (shaddah), meaning: "He barred them from the way, so that they would not prostrate," and so the preposition is omitted before "an" (that). It is also possible that "lā" is extra (zā'idah), and the meaning would be: "they are not guided, except that they prostrate."

The third is the reading of the codex of ʿAbd Allāh (Ibn Masʿūd), and the reading of al-Aʿmash: "hallā" (هلا), with the hamzah changed to a hā'. And from ʿAbd Allāh (it is also reported) "hallā tasjudūna," with the meaning of "alā tasjudūna" in the second person.

The fourth is the reading of Ubayy: "alā yasjudūna lillāhi alladhī yukhriju al-khab'a fī al-samāwāti wa al-arḍi wa yaʿlamu sirrakum wa mā tuʿlinūna."

The second issue: The people of verification (ahl al-taḥqīq) said: His statement ﴿alā yasjudū﴾ must be in the sense of a command, because if it were in the sense of prohibiting them from prostration, it would not have a description of Him that necessitates that prostration be due to Him, which is His being capable of bringing forth what is hidden and knowing secrets, a meaning.

* * *

The third issue: The verse indicates the attribution to Allah, exalted is He, of power and knowledge. As for power, it is His statement: ﴿who brings forth what is hidden in the heavens and the earth﴾, where what is hidden is named by the verbal noun (maṣdar), and it encompasses all kinds of provisions and wealth; its bringing forth from the sky is by rain, and from the earth by plants. As for knowledge, it is His statement: ﴿and knows what you conceal and what you disclose﴾.

Know that the purpose of this speech is a refutation of those who worship the sun. The reasoning is set out thus: God must be capable of bringing forth what is hidden and knowing hidden things, and the sun is not like that; therefore it is not a god, and if it is not a god, it is not permissible to prostrate to it. As for the fact that He, glorified and exalted, must be capable and knowing in the aforementioned manner, since He is necessary in His essence, His capability and knowledge are not restricted to some of the objects of power and knowledge to the exclusion of others. As for the fact that the sun is not like that, it is because it is a finite body, and whatever is finite in essence is finite in attributes; and if that is so, then it cannot be known that it is capable of bringing forth what is hidden and knowing hidden things. If it is not known of its state that this is so, then it is not known of its state that it is capable of bringing benefits and warding off harms. For Abraham said: ﴿My Lord is He who gives life and causes death﴾, then said: ﴿Indeed, Allah brings the sun from the east﴾; and Moses, peace be upon him, said: ﴿Your Lord and the Lord of your forefathers, the first ones﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 26], then said: ﴿Lord of the east and the west﴾. Why, then, is the order reversed here, so that the heavens' hidden things are placed before the earth's hidden things?

The answer: Abraham and Moses, peace be upon them both, were debating with one who claimed divinity for humans, so they inevitably began by refuting the divinity of humans, then moved on to refuting the divinity of the heavens. Here, however, the debate is with one who claimed divinity for the sun, as in His statement: ﴿I found her and her people prostrating to the sun instead of Allah﴾ [al-Naml: 24]; so inevitably He began by mentioning the celestial things, then the terrestrial things.

As for His statement: ﴿Allah—there is no deity except Him, Lord of the Mighty Throne﴾, what is meant by it is that when He, glorified is He, had explained the need of the heavens and the earth and what lies between them for a governor, He then mentioned that the greatest of bodies are created and nurtured, and this indicates that He, glorified is He, is the ultimate in power and lordship, to which nothing can be added. And Allah knows best.

The fourth issue: It has been said that from "I have encompassed" (aḥaṭtu) to "the Mighty" (al-ʿaẓīm) is the speech of the hoopoe, and it has been said that it is the speech of the Lord of Majesty.

* * *

The fifth issue: The truth is that the prostration of recitation is obligatory in both readings, and this is the view of al-Shafiʿi and Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on them both, because they agreed that the prostrations of the Qur'an are fourteen prostrations, and this is one of them. Also, the places of prostration are either a command to perform it, or praise for one who performs it, or blame for one who abandons it. One of the two readings is a command to prostrate, and the other is blame for the one who abandons it. Thus it is established that what al-Zajjaj mentioned regarding the obligation of prostration with the light reading, but not with the emphatic reading, is not worth considering.

The sixth issue: It may be asked: Does the one who stops differentiate between the two readings? The answer: Yes. If he reads with light stress, he stops at ﴿fa-hum lā yahtadūn﴾ (so they are not guided), then begins with "alā yasjudū"; and if he wishes, he stops at "alā yā," then begins with "usjudū." If he reads with emphatic stress, he does not stop except at "al-ʿarsh al-ʿaẓīm" (the Mighty Throne).

As for His statement: ﴿sananẓuru﴾ (We will see), it derives from "naẓar," which is reflection. The intended meaning is: "whether you have told the truth or lied." However, ﴿am kunta mina al-kādhibīn﴾ (or were you among the liars) is more emphatic, because if he was known for lying, he would be suspected of lying in what he reports, and so he would not be trusted. He said ﴿fa-alqihi ilayhim﴾ (deliver it to them) in the plural form, because he had said: ﴿I found her and her people prostrating to the sun﴾, so he said: ﴿deliver it to them﴾, meaning to those whose religion this is.

As for His statement: ﴿thumma tawalla ʿanhum﴾ (then withdraw from them), it means: move away from them to a nearby place where you can hide, so that what they say may be within your hearing. And ﴿yarji'ūn﴾ (they return) is from His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Some of them turn back to others in speech﴾ [Saba': 31]. It is said: he entered upon her through a window (kuwwah), threw the letter to her, and hid himself in the window.

[p. 167]

The Exalted said: ﴿She said, "O chiefs, indeed there has been delivered to me a noble letter."﴾ ﴿Indeed it is from Solomon, and indeed it reads: In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.﴾ ﴿Do not exalt yourselves over me, but come to me in submission.﴾ ﴿She said, "O chiefs, advise me in my affair. I would not decide an affair until you are present."﴾ ﴿They said, "We are possessed of strength and possessed of great might, but the command is yours, so consider what you will command."﴾

Know that His saying ﴿She said, "O chiefs, indeed there has been delivered to me a noble letter."﴾ has the sense that it is said: the hoopoe (al-Hudhud) delivered the letter to her. The object is omitted, as though it were stated. It is related that when she slept she would lock the doors and place the keys under her head. The hoopoe entered through a window (kuwwah) and dropped the letter onto her chest while she was lying on her back. It is also said that he pecked her, and she woke up startled.

As for His saying ﴿a noble letter﴾, there are three aspects to it:
The first: the goodness of its content and what it contains.
The second: its description as "noble" because it came from a noble king.
The third: the letter was sealed. The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "Its seal ennobled the letter." He (peace be upon him) used to write to the non-Arabs (al-ʿajam), and it was said to him: "They will not accept a letter unless it bears a seal," so he made a seal for himself.

As for His saying ﴿Indeed it is from Solomon, and indeed it reads: In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.﴾, there are several discussions:

The first discussion: It is a resumptive clause (istiʾnaf, a new sentence that resumes and explains) clarifying what was delivered to her. It is as though, when she said ﴿indeed there has been delivered to me a noble letter﴾, she was asked: "From whom is it, and what is it?" So she said: "Indeed it is from Solomon, and indeed it says such-and-such." ʿAbd Allah (Ibn Masʿud) read ﴿indeed it is from Solomon, and indeed it reads: In the name of God﴾ as a conjunction (ʿatf) with ﴿indeed (innī)﴾. It is also read ﴿that it is from Solomon, and that it﴾ with a fatḥah (anna). In this reading there are two possibilities:
One: it is a substitute (badal, apposition) for "letter," as if it were said: "There has been delivered to me that it is from Solomon."
The second: she intends that it is from Solomon, and because it begins with "In the name of God," as though she were giving as the reason for its nobility that it is from Solomon and that it opens with "In the name of God." Ubayy read ﴿that it is from Solomon, and that in the name of God﴾ with the explanatory "an" (al-mufassirah, the particle introducing an explanation). The "an" in ﴿that do not exalt yourselves﴾ is also explanatory. The meaning of ﴿do not exalt yourselves﴾ is: do not be arrogant as kings are. Ibn ʿAbbas read it with a ghayn (ghayn with a dot), from ghuluww, which is exceeding the limit.

The second discussion: It may be asked why Solomon placed his name before ﴿In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate﴾. The answer: far be it from him to do that. Rather, he himself began with "In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate." Bilqis only mentioned that this letter was from Solomon and then related what was in the letter. God the Exalted related it that way, so the precedence occurs within the narration.

The third discussion: Prophets (peace be upon them) do not lengthen their speech but confine themselves to the purpose. This letter contains the full purpose, because what is required of creation is either knowledge or action, and knowledge takes precedence over action. So His saying ﴿In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate﴾ contains the affirmation of the Creator, glory be to Him and exalted, and the affirmation that He is Knowing, Powerful, Living, Willing, Wise and Merciful.

* * *

As for His saying ﴿Do not exalt yourselves over me﴾, it is a prohibition against yielding to the obedience of the self, desire, and arrogance.

* * *

As for His saying ﴿but come to me in submission﴾, the meaning of "muslim" is either one who submits or one who believes. Thus it is established that this letter, despite its brevity, contains everything necessary in religion and worldly life. If it is objected: the prohibition against domineering and the command to submit, before establishing the proof that he is a true messenger, indicates reliance on imitation (taqlid). The answer: God forbid that there was any imitation there. The messenger of Solomon to Bilqis was the hoopoe, and the message of the hoopoe was a miracle (muʿjiz, a miraculous sign). A miracle indicates the existence of the Creator and His attributes, and indicates the truthfulness of the claimant. Since that message was a complete proof of monotheism and prophethood, it is certain that he did not mention any other proof in the letter.

As for His saying ﴿O chiefs, advise me in my affair﴾, the word fatwā means the answer to an incident. It is derived metaphorically from fatī (young, in age), meaning: answer me concerning the youthful matter. By consulting them and seeking their opinion, she intended to comfort their hearts. ﴿I would not decide an affair﴾ means: I will not settle any matter except in your presence.

As for His saying ﴿They said, "We are possessed of strength"﴾, the intended meaning is strength of bodies and strength of instruments. "Might" (baʾs) means valor and steadfastness in war. The summary of their answer is that the people mentioned two things:
One: displaying their inherent and acquired strength, so that it would be clear that if she wanted them for defense and war, she would find them ready for what she wishes.
The other: their saying ﴿but the command is yours, so consider what you will command﴾. In this is a display of obedience to her if she desires peace. No better answer than this can be given, and God knows best.

The third: the letter was sealed. The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "Its seal ennobled the letter." He (peace be upon him) used to write to the non-Arabs (al-ʿajam), and it was said to him: "They will not accept a letter unless it bears a seal," so he made a seal for himself.

As for His saying ﴿Indeed it is from Solomon, and indeed it reads: In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.﴾, there are several discussions:

The first discussion: It is a resumptive clause (istiʾnaf, a new sentence that resumes and explains) clarifying what was delivered to her. It is as though, when she said ﴿indeed there has been delivered to me a noble letter﴾, she was asked: "From whom is it, and what is it?" So she said: "Indeed it is from Solomon, and indeed it says such-and-such." ʿAbd Allah (Ibn Masʿud) read ﴿indeed it is from Solomon, and indeed it reads: In the name of God﴾ as a conjunction (ʿatf) with ﴿indeed (innī)﴾. It is also read ﴿that it is from Solomon, and that it﴾ with a fatḥah (anna). In this reading there are two possibilities:
One: it is a substitute (badal, apposition) for "letter," as if it were said: "There has been delivered to me that it is from Solomon."
The second: she intends that it is from Solomon, and because it begins with "In the name of God," as though she were giving as the reason for its nobility that it is from Solomon and that it opens with "In the name of God." Ubayy read ﴿that it is from Solomon, and that in the name of God﴾ with the explanatory "an" (al-mufassirah, the particle introducing an explanation). The "an" in ﴿that do not exalt yourselves﴾ is also explanatory. The meaning of ﴿do not exalt yourselves﴾ is: do not be arrogant as kings are. Ibn ʿAbbas read it with a ghayn (ghayn with a dot), from ghuluww, which is exceeding the limit.

The second discussion: It may be asked why Solomon placed his name before ﴿In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate﴾. The answer: far be it from him to do that. Rather, he himself began with "In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate." Bilqis only mentioned that this letter was from Solomon and then related what was in the letter. God the Exalted related it that way, so the precedence occurs within the narration.

The third discussion: Prophets (peace be upon them) do not lengthen their speech but confine themselves to the purpose. This letter contains the full purpose, because what is required of creation is either knowledge or action, and knowledge takes precedence over action. So His saying ﴿In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate﴾ contains the affirmation of the Creator, glory be to Him and exalted, and the affirmation that He is Knowing, Powerful, Living, Willing, Wise and Merciful.

* * *

As for His saying ﴿Do not exalt yourselves over me﴾, it is a prohibition against yielding to the obedience of the self, desire, and arrogance.

* * *

As for His saying ﴿but come to me in submission﴾, the meaning of "muslim" is either one who submits or one who believes. Thus it is established that this letter, despite its brevity, contains everything necessary in religion and worldly life. If it is objected: the prohibition against domineering and the command to submit, before establishing the proof that he is a true messenger, indicates reliance on imitation (taqlid). The answer: God forbid that there was any imitation there. The messenger of Solomon to Bilqis was the hoopoe, and the message of the hoopoe was a miracle (muʿjiz, a miraculous sign). A miracle indicates the existence of the Creator and His attributes, and indicates the truthfulness of the claimant. Since that message was a complete proof of monotheism and prophethood, it is certain that he did not mention any other proof in the letter.

As for His saying ﴿O chiefs, advise me in my affair﴾, the word fatwā means the answer to an incident. It is derived metaphorically from fatī (young, in age), meaning: answer me concerning the youthful matter. By consulting them and seeking their opinion, she intended to comfort their hearts. ﴿I would not decide an affair﴾ means: I will not settle any matter except in your presence.

As for His saying ﴿They said, "We are possessed of strength"﴾, the intended meaning is strength of bodies and strength of instruments. "Might" (baʾs) means valor and steadfastness in war. The summary of their answer is that the people mentioned two things:
One: displaying their inherent and acquired strength, so that it would be clear that if she wanted them for defense and war, she would find them ready for what she wishes.
The other: their saying ﴿but the command is yours, so consider what you will command﴾. In this is a display of obedience to her if she desires peace. No better answer than this can be given, and God knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 27, verse 34–37:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿She said: "Indeed, when kings enter a town, they corrupt it and make the most honorable of its people the most humble. And thus do they do."﴾ ﴿"And indeed, I am going to send them a gift, and I will wait to see what the envoys return with."﴾ ﴿So when he came to Sulayman, he said, "Will you provide me with wealth? What Allah has given me is better than what He has given you. Rather, you rejoice in your gift."﴾ ﴿"Return to them, for we will surely come to them with soldiers they cannot resist, and we will surely expel them from it in humiliation, and they will be debased."﴾

Know that when she presented the matter to the notables of her people and they said what preceded, she revealed her opinion, which is that when kings enter a town by force, they corrupt it, that is, they ruin it and humble its honorable ones. So she mentioned to them the consequence of war.

* * *
As for His saying: ﴿And thus do they do﴾, the scholars differed over whether it is part of her speech or part of the speech of Allah exalted, as an affirmation of her. The more likely view is that it is part of her speech, and that she mentioned it as an emphasis on what she had described of the condition of kings. As for the discussion of the nature of the gift, people have said much about it, but there is no mention of it in the Book. Her saying: ﴿and I will wait to see what the envoys return with﴾ indicates that she did not feel confident about acceptance and allowed for rejection, and by this she intended that the aim of Sulayman be revealed to her. When the gifts reached Sulayman, peace be upon him, he mentioned two matters:

The first: his saying: ﴿Will you provide me with wealth?﴾ By this statement he showed his lack of concern for that wealth.

As for his saying: ﴿Rather, you rejoice in your gift﴾, there are three aspects to it:

One of them: that "gift" (hadiyyah) is a name for the thing given, just as "gift" (atiyyah) is a name for the thing bestowed, so it may be attributed to the giver and to the recipient, and the attributed term here is the one to whom the gift is given. The meaning is that Allah exalted gave me the religion, which is the highest happiness, and gave me of the world what admits no increase; so how could one like me be enticed by such a gift? Rather, you rejoice in what is given to you, but my condition is the opposite of yours.

The second: "Rather, you rejoice in this gift of yours which you have sent, because you were able to send the like of it."

The third: it is as if he said: "Rather, it is your right to take your gift and rejoice in it."

The second matter: his saying: ﴿Return to them﴾. It was said: "Return" is addressed to the messenger, and it was said: it is addressed to the hoopoe, carrying another letter.

As for His saying exalted: ﴿no power (qibal)﴾, meaning no ability; the real sense of qibal is resistance and confrontation, that is, they will not be able to face them. Ibn Mas'ud read: "la qibala lahum bihim," and the pronoun in "minha" refers to Saba'. Humiliation (dhull) is that what they had of honor and kingship be taken away from them, and debasement (sagar) is that they fall into captivity and servitude, and it is not limited to their becoming commoners after having been kings.

[Page 169]

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿He said, "O chiefs, which of you will bring me her throne before they come to me in submission?"﴾ ﴿A powerful one among the jinn said, "I will bring it to you before you rise from your place. Indeed I am strong and trustworthy for it."﴾ ﴿One who had knowledge of the Scripture said, "I will bring it to you before your glance returns to you." And when he saw it settled beside him, he said, "This is from the bounty of my Lord, to test me whether I will be grateful or ungrateful. And whoever is grateful, his gratitude is only for his own self; and whoever is ungrateful, indeed my Lord is Self-Sufficient and Generous."﴾

Know that in His saying, the Exalted, ﴿He said, "O chiefs, which of you will bring me her throne"﴾, there is an indication that she had resolved to join Sulayman, and an indication that the matter of that throne was well known, so he wished to have it present with him before her arrival. The scholars differed concerning Sulayman's (peace be upon him) purpose in bringing that throne, in several respects:

The first: that the aim was for it to be a sign for Bilqis of the power of Allah the Exalted and of the prophethood of Sulayman (peace be upon him), so that this sign would be added to the other proofs that had preceded.

The second: he intended that the throne be brought, altered and disguised, then presented to her, so that he could see whether she would recognize it or deny it. The aim was to test her intellect. His saying, the Exalted, ﴿He said, "Disguise her throne for her; we shall see whether she is guided"﴾ [an-Naml: 41] serves as an indication of this.

The third: Qatadah said he intended to take it before her conversion, knowing that once she embraced Islam it would not be lawful for him to take her property.

The fourth: the throne is the seat of kingship, so he wanted to learn the extent of her kingdom before her arrival to him.

As for His saying, ﴿A powerful one among the jinn said﴾, the "ifrit" (ʿifrīt) among men is the wicked, defiant one who subdues his peers, and among the devils it is the wicked, rebellious one.

As for His saying, ﴿before you rise from your place﴾, the meaning is "from your sitting place." It must have a known customary practice so that a time can be set by it. It was said: the intended meaning is the seat of judgment among the people. It was said: the time at which he addresses the people. It was said: until midday.

* * *

As for His saying, ﴿indeed I am strong﴾, meaning, "capable of carrying it," ﴿and trustworthy﴾, "I will bring it to you as it is, without diminishing anything from it."

As for His saying, ﴿One who had knowledge of the Scripture said﴾, there are two discussions concerning it:

The first: the scholars differed about that person, on two views. It was said he was an angel, and it was said he was a human. Those who held the first view differed: it was said he was Jibril (peace be upon him), and it was said he was an angel whom Allah the Exalted strengthened to assist Sulayman (peace be upon him). Those who held the second view differed in several respects:

The first: the saying of Ibn Mas'ud, that he was al-Khadir (peace be upon him).

The second: and this is the well-known saying of Ibn Abbas: that he was Asaf ibn Barkhiya, the minister of Sulayman, who was a truthful man who knew the Greatest Name (al-ism al-aʿẓam), such that when he called upon it he was answered.

The third: the saying of Qatadah: a man from mankind who knew the Greatest Name of Allah.

The fourth: the saying of Ibn Zayd: he was a righteous man on an island in the sea, who came out that day to look at Sulayman.

The fifth: rather, he was Sulayman himself, and the one addressed is the ʿifrīt who spoke to him. Sulayman (peace be upon him) intended to display a miracle, so he first challenged them, then made clear to the ʿifrīt that he could achieve, through the swiftness of bringing the throne, what the ʿifrīt could not. This view is closer for several reasons:

The first: the word "alladhī" (the one who) is used in the language to point to a specific person when seeking to identify him through a known story. The person known to have "knowledge of the Scripture" is Sulayman (peace be upon him), so it is necessary to direct the expression to him. At most one might say Asaf was likewise; but we say that Sulayman (peace be upon him) knew the Scripture better than he did, because he is the Prophet, so directing this expression to Sulayman (peace be upon him) is more appropriate.

The second: bringing the throne in that subtle moment is a lofty rank, so if it had been granted to Asaf rather than Sulayman, that would imply the preference of Asaf over Sulayman (peace be upon him), and that is not permissible.

The third: if Sulayman (peace be upon him) had needed, for this, some attribute, that would imply the inferiority of Sulayman's standing in the eyes of creation.

The fourth: Sulayman said, ﴿This is from the bounty of my Lord, to test me whether I will be grateful or ungrateful﴾, and its apparent meaning requires that this miraculous act was brought about by Allah the Exalted in response to Sulayman's supplication.

The second discussion: the scholars differed concerning "the Scripture." It was said: it is the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz), and the one who had knowledge of it was Jibril (peace be upon him). It was said: it is the book of Sulayman, or the book of some of the prophets. It is known in general that this is a praise, and that this attribute had an effect in transporting that throne. Therefore they said: it is the Greatest Name, and that with it the response from Allah the Exalted came in the swiftest time.

As for His saying, the Exalted, ﴿I will bring it to you before your glance returns to you﴾, there are two discussions concerning it:

The first: "ātīka" (I bring you) in both places may be a verb or an active participle.

The second: the scholars differed concerning His saying, ﴿before your glance returns to you﴾, on two views:

The first: that it intends exaggeration in speed, as when you say to your companion, "Do that in a blink," and this is the saying of Mujahid.

The second: that it is to be taken literally. The "ṭarf" is the movement of the eyelids when looking. When you open the eyelid, one may imagine that the light of the eye extends to the object seen; and when you close the eyelid, one may imagine that this light returns to the eye. This is what is meant by the "return of the glance."

Here there is a question: how is it possible, given the great distance, to transport the throne in such a short time? This implies either the affirmation of the leap (ṭafrah, instantaneous transfer across space) or the existence of one body in two places at once. The answer: the geometers said that the sphere of the sun is one hundred and sixty-four times the sphere of the earth, and that the time of its rising is short. If we divide the time of the full disc's rising by the time of the distance between al-Sham and Yemen, the "lamḥah" (instant) becomes many times over. Since it is established by reason that such rapid motion is possible, and since it is established that He the Exalted is capable of all possible things, the question is removed.

Then, when he ﴿saw it settled beside him, he said, "This is from the bounty of my Lord, to test me whether I will be grateful or ungrateful."﴾ The discussion of the meaning of "ibtila'" (testing) has passed more than once. Then he (peace be upon him) made clear that the benefit of gratitude returns to the one who is grateful, not to Allah the Exalted. As for its return to the grateful one, there are several reasons:

The first: he discharges what was obligatory upon him of gratitude.

The second: he seeks increase by it, in accordance with His saying: ﴿If you are grateful, I will surely increase you﴾ [Ibrahim: 7].

The third: the one occupied with gratitude is occupied with sensory pleasures, and the difference between them is like the difference between the Benefactor and the blessing in nobility.

Then He said, ﴿And whoever is ungrateful, indeed my Lord is Self-Sufficient and Generous﴾: Self-Sufficient, independent of his gratitude, whose ingratitude does not harm Him; Generous, who does not cut off His blessings from him because of his turning away from gratitude.

The third: the saying of Qatadah: a man from mankind who knew the Greatest Name of Allah.

The fourth: the saying of Ibn Zayd: he was a righteous man on an island in the sea, who came out that day to look at Sulayman.

The first: "ātīka" (I bring you) in both places may be a verb or an active participle.

The second: the scholars differed concerning His saying, ﴿before your glance returns to you﴾, on two views:

The first: that it intends exaggeration in speed, as when you say to your companion, "Do that in a blink," and this is the saying of Mujahid.

The second: that it is to be taken literally. The "ṭarf" is the movement of the eyelids when looking. Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 27, verses 41–43:

Page 171

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿He said: "Disguise her throne for her; we shall see whether she will be guided or whether she will be among those who are not guided."﴾ ﴿So when she came, it was said, "Is your throne like this?" She said, "It is as if it were it." "And we were given the knowledge before her, and we were Muslims."﴾ ﴿And that which she used to worship besides Allah had prevented her; indeed, she was of a disbelieving people.﴾

Know that His saying ﴿nakkirū﴾ (disguise) means: make the throne unrecognizable, changed from its form, just as a man disguises himself before people so that they will not recognize him. That is because if it were left as it was, she would undoubtedly recognize it, and her recognition of it would not indicate the soundness of her intellect. But when it was changed, her recognition of it or her hesitation regarding it indicates superiority of intellect. There is no impossibility in the validity of what has been said: that Solomon, upon him be peace, was informed that she had a deficiency of intellect, so that he would not marry her, or so that she would not find favor with him out of envy; so he intended by what we have mentioned to test her intellect.

As for His saying ﴿nanẓur﴾ (we shall see), it has been read with the jussive (*jazm*) as an answer (*jawāb*), and with the nominative (*raf'*) as a resumed sentence (*isti'nāf*). The scholars differed regarding (*atahtadī*, "will you be guided") in two ways:

The first: "Will you recognize that it is your throne or not?" as we have previously mentioned.

The second: "Will you recognize through it the prophethood of Solomon or not?" For this reason He said: ﴿or will you be among those who are not guided?﴾ This is like a reproach, and it is only appropriate in the manner of an indication. So it is as if he, upon him be peace, wished that she would look and thereby recognize his prophethood, from the fact that it had moved from the distant place to there, and this indicates the power of Allah the Exalted and the truthfulness of Solomon, upon him be peace. She would also thereby recognize the superiority of her intellect for purposes he had in mind. At that point he questioned her.

As for His saying ﴿Is your throne like this?﴾, know that *hākadhā* (like this) consists of three words: the particle of alerting (*harf al-tanbīh*), the particle of comparison (*kāf al-tashbīh*), and the demonstrative noun (*ism al-ishārah*). He did not say, "Is this your throne?" but rather, "Is the likeness of this your throne?" so that it would not be a prompting. So she said ﴿It is as if it were it﴾, and she did not say, "It is it," nor "It is not it." That is from the perfection of her intellect, in that she hesitated at the place of hesitation.

As for His saying ﴿and we were given the knowledge before her﴾, there are two questions concerning it: whose speech is this? And upon what is this statement conjoined? There are two answers to it:

The first: that it is the speech of Solomon and his people. That is because when Bilqis was asked about her throne, and then she answered with her saying ﴿It is as if it were it﴾, the apparent meaning is that Solomon and his people said: she has been correct in her answer, and she is intelligent and sagacious, and she has been granted Islam. Then they conjoined to that their saying: "We were given knowledge of Allah and His power before her knowledge," and their purpose in that is to give thanks to Allah the Exalted for having singled them out with the distinction of precedence in Islam.

The second: that it is from the speech of Bilqis, joined to her saying ﴿It is as if it were it﴾, and the meaning is: "We were given the knowledge of Allah and of the validity of Solomon's prophethood before this miracle, or before this situation." Then His saying ﴿And that which she used to worship besides Allah had prevented her﴾ up to the end of the verse is from the speech of the Lord of Majesty.

As for His saying Exalted is He ﴿And that which she used to worship besides Allah had prevented her﴾, there are two possibilities regarding it:

The first: the meaning is: her worship of other than Allah prevented her from faith.

The second: Allah or Solomon prevented her from what she used to worship, by way of omitting the preposition and making the verb reach its object. It was also read *annahā* with a fatḥah, as a substitute (*badal*) for the subject of *ṣadda*, and with the meaning of *li-annahā* ("because she"). The Mu'tazilah took this verse as evidence, saying: if Exalted Allah had created disbelief in her, then what prevented her would not be her former disbelief, nor her being among the disbelievers; rather, what would prevent her from faith would be the renewed creation by Allah of disbelief in her.

The answer: as for the second interpretation, there is no doubt that the argument falls away.

As for the first, our answer is: her being among the disbelievers became a cause for the arising of the motive that necessitates disbelief, and at that point the apparent meaning of the verse remains in agreement with our statement. And Allah knows best.

The Exalted said: ﴿It was said to her, "Enter the palace." But when she saw it, she thought it was a pool of water and bared her shins. He said, "It is a palace paved with glass." She said, "My Lord, I have wronged myself, and I submit with Solomon to Allah, Lord of the worlds."﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, related her persistence in disbelief despite all the proofs mentioned earlier, He mentioned that Solomon, peace be upon him, displayed a matter that became a call for her to embrace Islam. This is His saying: ﴿It was said to her, "Enter the palace."﴾ *Al-sarh* (ٱلصَّرْح) means the palace, as in His saying: ﴿O Haman, build me a tower﴾ [Ghafir: 36]. It was also said that it means the courtyard of the house.

Ibn Kathir read *"sa'qayha"* (سَأْقَيْها) with a hamza. The reason for this is that he heard *su'q* (سُؤْق), and so he treated it as the singular form.

*Al-mumarrad* means the smooth, polished thing. It is narrated that Solomon, peace be upon him, ordered before her arrival that a palace be built for him on her route, made of white glass as clear as water. Then he sent water beneath it, put fish and other creatures in it, and placed his throne in its middle, and he sat upon it. Humans, jinn and birds gathered around him. He did this only to increase her awe of his affair and to confirm his prophethood for her.

They claimed that the jinn disliked his marrying her, lest she reveal their secrets to him, because she was the daughter of a jinn woman. It was also said that they feared that a child might be born to him from her, which would combine the cleverness of the jinn and of humans, so that they would leave Solomon's dominion for a dominion that is stronger. Therefore they said that there was a deficiency in her intellect, that she had hairy shins, and that her foot was like a donkey's hoof. So Solomon tested her intellect by altering the throne, and he built the palace so that he could learn about her shin. It is well known that clear glass is like water, so when she saw that, she thought it was still water and bared her shins in order to wade through it. Then, behold, she had the most beautiful shins and feet of all people.

This is according to the view of those who say that he married her. Others said that the purpose of the palace was to overawe and magnify the assembly, and that the baring of her shins happened incidentally. When it was said to her, "It is a palace paved with glass," she covered herself, was amazed at this, and took it as evidence for monotheism and prophethood. So she said: ﴿My Lord, I have wronged myself﴾ regarding what had preceded, by persisting in disbelief. Then she said: ﴿and I submit with Solomon to Allah, Lord of the worlds.﴾

It was also said that she thought Solomon, peace be upon him, would drown her in the deep water, so she said: "I have wronged myself by my bad opinion of Solomon."

Scholars differed over whether he married her or not, and whether he married her in this state or before she bared her shins. The more apparent view among people is that he married her, but there is no mention of this in the Book, nor in any report whose authenticity is definitively established.

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that when she embraced Islam, he said to her, "Choose from your people whomever I should marry you to." She said, "One like me does not marry men while I have my authority." He said, "Marriage is part of Islam." She said, "If that is so, then marry me to Dhu Tubba', king of Hamdan." So he married her to him, then returned them both to Yemen, and she remained a queen there. And Allah knows best.

It was recited (ۤanna u'budu Allah) with a ḍamma on the nūn, following the bāʾ (the vowel of the nūn is assimilated to the following bāʾ's ḍamma), as a variant recitation (qira'a).

As for His words, ﴿then they were two factions﴾, there are two opinions:
One: the intended meaning is a believing faction and a disbelieving faction.
Two: the intended meaning is the people of Salih before any of them had believed.

As for His words, ﴿contending with each other﴾, the meaning is: those who believed only believed because they examined his proof and recognised its soundness. If that is so, there must be an opponent to those who did not accept it. And if this contention is in matters of religion, this indicates that disputation in matters of religion is valid and that it nullifies blind imitation (taqlīd).

As for His words, ﴿He said, "O my people, why do you seek to hasten evil before good?"﴾, there are two discussions.

The first: concerning the explanation of hastening evil before good, there are two views:
One: when those who denied Salih (peace be upon him) found that argument did not benefit them, Salih (peace be upon him) threatened them with punishment. They said, mockingly, ﴿Bring us the punishment of Allah if you are among the truthful﴾ (Al-ʿAnkabūt: 29). At this, Salih said, ﴿Why do you seek to hasten evil before good?﴾ The meaning is: Allah has enabled you to reach His mercy and reward, so why do you turn away from that to hasten His punishment?
Second: they were saying, out of their ignorance, that if the punishment that Salih promised befell them, as he claimed, then they would come and seek forgiveness, and then Allah would accept their repentance and avert the punishment from them. So Salih addressed them according to their own belief and said: Why do you not seek Allah's forgiveness before the punishment descends? For hastening towards good is better than hastening towards evil.

[Page 174]

The second discussion: the intended meaning of "evil" (sayyi'a) is punishment and the intended meaning of "good" (ḥasana) is reward. As for describing punishment as "evil," this is a metaphor (majāz), and the reason for this figurative usage is either that punishment is among the necessary consequences of evil, or that it resembles evil in being disliked. As for describing mercy as "good," some say it is literal (ḥaqīqa) and some say it is figurative, and the first is closer to the truth.

Then, when Salih (peace be upon him) had established this true statement, they answered him with a false statement, which is their saying, ﴿We consider you a bad omen﴾, meaning: we take you as an omen of ill fortune (tashā'amnā), because the hardship and drought that afflicts us comes from your ill omen and the ill omen of those with you.

The author of al-Kashshāf said: A man would set out on a journey and pass by a bird and drive it away; if it passed on his right (sānih), he would take it as an omen of good, and if it passed on his left (bāriḥ), he would take it as an omen of ill. When they attributed good and evil to the bird, the term was borrowed for what was actually the cause of good and evil, which is the decree and apportionment of Allah. So Salih (peace be upon him) answered with His words, ﴿Your omen is with Allah﴾, meaning the cause from which your good and your evil come is with Allah, namely His judgement and decree: if He wills, He provides for you, and if He wills, He withholds from you. It was also said: rather, the meaning is that the consequence of your ill omen from you is with Allah, which is punishment; but the first view is closer, because the people pointed to a matter that had actually occurred, so the answer must concern that matter and not something else. Then He made clear that this was their ignorance, by His words, ﴿rather, you are a people being tested﴾. It is possible that others induced them to this statement, and it is possible that the meaning is that Satan tests you through his whisperings.

Then He, glorified be He, said, ﴿And there were in the city nine men who spread corruption in the land﴾. The closer view is that the intended meaning is nine groups, since the apparent meaning of "rahṭ" is a group and not a single individual. It is possible that they were tribes, and it is possible that they were grouped under this number because of differences in their qualities and conditions, not because of differences in their cause. So Allah, exalted is He, made clear that they spread corruption in the land and did not mix that corruption with any reform, and for this reason He said, ﴿who spread corruption in the land and did not reform﴾. Then He, exalted is He, made clear that among that corruption was what they intended concerning the affair of Salih (peace be upon him).

As for His words, ﴿Swear to one another by Allah﴾, it may be an imperative, or a statement in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), with "qad" understood (ḥāl (circumstantial accusative) with an implied qad), meaning: they said, swearing to one another. And "bayāt" means attacking the enemy by night.

As for His words, ﴿then we will say to his heir, "We did not witness the destruction of his family"﴾, the meaning is: if his people accused us, we would swear to them that we were not present. It was recited as "mahlaka" with a fatḥa on the mīm and lām, and with a kasra on the mīm... from halaka; and "muhlak" with a ḍamma on the mīm, from ahlaka. It may be a verbal noun, a place, or a time.

Then He, exalted is He, said, ﴿And they plotted a plot, and We plotted a plot, while they were unaware.﴾ Scholars have differed regarding the plotting of Allah, exalted is He, in several ways:
One: the plot of Allah is their destruction from a direction they were not aware of. It is likened to the plot of a plotter by way of metaphor. It is related that Salih (peace be upon him) had a mosque in al-Ḥijr, in a mountain pass, where he would pray. They said: Salih claims that he will be done with us within three days, so we will be done with him and his family before the three days are over. So they went out to the pass and said: when he comes to pray, we will kill him; then we will return to his family and kill them. But Allah, exalted is He, sent a rock which sealed the mouth of the pass over them, so they perished, and the rest perished by the Cry.
Second: they came at night with their swords drawn, and Allah, exalted is He, had sent the angels to fill the house of Salih, and they struck them with stones; they saw the stones but did not see the one who threw them.
Third: Allah, exalted is He, informed Salih of their plot, so he took precautions against them. That is the plot of Allah, exalted is He, against them.

As for His words, ﴿that We destroyed them﴾, it is a resumptive new sentence (isti'nāf). Whoever reads it with a fatḥa (anna) treats it as a substitute for "ʿāqiba" (outcome), or as the predicate of an omitted subject whose estimate is: it (the outcome) destroys them; or he puts it in the accusative with the sense of "because we," or as the predicate of "kāna" (was), meaning: the outcome of their plot was destruction.

[Page 175]

As for His words, ﴿empty﴾ (khāwiya), it is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl), governed by what is indicated by "tilka" (those). ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar recited "khāwiyatun" with a ḍamma, as the predicate of the omitted subject. And Allah knows best.

But among the commentators some have said that they said this only mockingly. Then He, exalted is He, made clear that He saved him and his family, except his wife, and destroyed the rest. All of this has already been explained in detail. Here ends the stories in this surah, and Allah knows best.

**On Allah's address to Muhammad (ﷺ)**

The words of the Exalted: ﴿Say, "Praise be to Allah, and peace upon His servants whom He has chosen. Is Allah better, or what they associate?"﴾

On this verse there are two views:
One: it is connected to what precedes it of the stories, and the meaning is: Praise be to Allah for their destruction, and peace upon His servants whom He chose, by sending them and saving them.
Two: it is a new beginning. When He, exalted is He, mentioned the conditions of the prophets (peace be upon them), and Muhammad (ﷺ) was like one who differs from those before him regarding the matter of punishment, since the punishment of total annihilation was lifted from his people, He commanded him to thank his Lord for what He had specially granted him of these blessings, and to offer peace upon the prophets (peace be upon them) who endured the hardships of the message.

As for His words, ﴿Is Allah better, or what they associate?﴾, it is a rebuke to the polytheists and a mockery of their state, because they preferred the worship of idols over the worship of Allah, exalted is He, and no rational person prefers one thing over another except for an increase in good or benefit. So this statement was addressed to them to draw attention to the extremity of their error and ignorance. It is also recited as "yushrikūna" with the yā' and with the tā' (ta'). It is related from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that whenever he recited it he would say: "Rather, Allah is better, more enduring, more exalted, and more generous."

Then know that He, glorified and exalted is He, spoke after this in a number of sections.

The First Section: Refutation of the Idol-Worshippers. The purpose of this section is to show that He, glory be to Him and exalted is He, is the Creator of the roots of blessings and their branches, so how could it be fitting to worship that from which no benefit whatsoever comes? Then He, glory be to Him and exalted is He, mentioned several kinds [of blessings]:

The first: concerning the explanation of hastening evil before good, there are two views:
One: when those who denied Salih (peace be upon him) found that argument did not benefit them, Salih (peace be upon him) threatened them with punishment. They said, mockingly, ﴿Bring us the punishment of Allah if you are among the truthful﴾ (Al-ʿAnkabūt: 29). At this, Salih said, ﴿Why do you seek to hasten evil before good?﴾ The meaning is: Allah has enabled you to reach His mercy and reward, so why do you turn away from that to hasten His punishment?

[Page 174]

As for describing punishment as "evil," this is a metaphor (majāz), and the reason for this figurative usage is either that punishment is among the necessary consequences of evil, or that it resembles evil in being disliked. As for describing mercy as "good," some say it is literal (ḥaqīqa) and some say it is figurative, and the first is closer to the truth.

Then, when Salih (peace be upon him) had established this true statement, they answered him with a false statement, which is their saying, ﴿We consider you a bad omen﴾, meaning: we take you as an omen of ill fortune (tashā'amnā), because the hardship and drought that afflicts us comes from your ill omen and the ill omen of those with you.

Then He, exalted is He, made clear that among that corruption was what they intended concerning the affair of Salih (peace be upon him).

It was recited as "mahlaka" with a fatḥa on the mīm and lām, and with a kasra on the mīm... from halaka; and "muhlak" with a ḍamma on the mīm, from ahlaka. It may be a verbal noun, a place, or a time.

Then He, exalted is He, said, ﴿And they plotted a plot, and We plotted a plot, while they were unaware.﴾ Scholars have differed regarding the plotting of Allah, exalted is He, in several ways:
One: the plot of Allah is their destruction from a direction they were not aware of. It is likened to the plot of a plotter by way of metaphor. It is related that Salih (peace be upon him) had a mosque in al-Ḥijr, in a mountain pass, where he would pray. The first: concerning the explanation of hastening evil before good, there are two views:
One: when those who denied Salih (peace be upon him) found that argument did not benefit them, Salih (peace be upon him) threatened them with punishment. They said, mockingly, ﴿Bring us the punishment of Allah if you are among the truthful﴾ (Al-ʿAnkabūt: 29). At this, Salih said, ﴿Why do you seek to hasten evil before good?﴾ The meaning is: Allah has enabled you to reach His mercy and reward, so why do you turn away from that to hasten His punishment?

[Page 174]

As for describing punishment as "evil," this is a metaphor (majāz), and the reason for this figurative usage is either that punishment is among the necessary consequences of evil, or that it resembles evil in being disliked. As for describing mercy as "good," some say it is literal (ḥaqīqa) and some say it is figurative, and the first is closer to the truth.

Then, when Salih (peace be upon him) had established this true statement, they answered him with a false statement, which is their saying, ﴿We consider you a bad omen﴾, meaning: we take you as an omen of ill fortune (tashā'amnā), because the hardship and drought that afflicts us comes from your ill omen and the ill omen of those with you.

Then He, exalted is He, made clear that among that corruption was what they intended concerning the affair of Salih (peace be upon him).

It was recited as "mahlaka" with a fatḥa on the mīm and lām, and with a kasra on the mīm... from halaka; and "muhlak" with a ḍamma on the mīm, from ahlaka. It may be a verbal noun, a place, or a time.

Then He, exalted is He, said, ﴿And they plotted a plot, and We plotted a plot, while they were unaware.﴾ Scholars have differed regarding the plotting of Allah, exalted is He, in several ways:
One: the plot of Allah is their destruction from a direction they were not aware of. It is likened to the plot of a plotter by way of metaphor. It is related that Salih (peace be upon him) had a mosque in al-Ḥijr, in a mountain pass, where he would pray. The first: concerning the explanation of hastening evil before good, there are two views:
One: when those who denied Salih (peace be upon him) found that argument did not benefit them, Salih (peace be upon him) threatened them with punishment. They said, mockingly, ﴿Bring us the punishment of Allah if you are among the truthful﴾ (Al-ʿAnkabūt: 29). At this, Salih said, ﴿Why do you seek to hasten evil before good?﴾ The meaning is: Allah has enabled you to reach His mercy and reward, so why do you turn away from that to hasten His punishment?

[Page 174]

As for describing punishment as "evil," this is a metaphor (majāz), and the reason for this figurative usage is either that punishment is among the necessary consequences of evil, or that it resembles evil in being disliked. As for describing mercy as "good," some say it is literal (ḥaqīqa) and some say it is figurative, and the first is closer to the truth.

Then, when Salih (peace be upon him) had established this true statement, they answered him with a false statement, which is their saying, ﴿We consider you a bad omen﴾, meaning: we take you as an omen of ill fortune (tashā'amnā), because the hardship and drought that afflicts us comes from your ill omen and the ill omen of those with you.

Then He, exalted is He, made clear that among that corruption was what they intended concerning the affair of Salih (peace be upon him).

It was recited as "mahlaka" with a fatḥa on the mīm and lām, and with a kasra on the mīm... from halaka; and "muhlak" with a ḍamma on the mīm, from ahlaka. It may be a verbal noun, a place, or a time.

Then He, exalted is He, said, ﴿And they plotted a plot, and We plotted a plot, while they were unaware.﴾ Scholars have differed regarding the plotting of Allah, exalted is He, in several ways:
One: the plot of Allah is their destruction from a direction they were not aware of. It is likened to the plot of a plotter by way of metaphor. It is related that Salih (peace be upon him) had a mosque in al-Ḥijr, in a mountain pass, where he would pray. The first: concerning the explanation of hastening evil before good, there are two views:
One: when those who denied Salih (peace be upon him) found that argument did not benefit them, Salih (peace be upon him) threatened them with punishment. They said, mockingly, ﴿Bring us the punishment of Allah if you are among the truthful﴾ (Al-ʿAnkabūt: 29). At this, Salih said, ﴿Why do you seek to hasten evil before good?﴾ The meaning is: Allah has enabled you to reach His mercy and reward, so why do you turn away from that to hasten His punishment?

[Page 174]

As for describing punishment as "evil," this is a metaphor (majāz), and the reason for this figurative usage is either that punishment is among the necessary consequences of evil, or that it resembles evil in being disliked. As for describing mercy as "good," some say it is literal (ḥaqīqa) and some say it is figurative, and the first is closer to the truth.

Then, when Salih (peace be upon him) had established this true statement, they answered him with a false statement, which is their saying, ﴿We consider you a bad omen﴾, meaning: we take you as an omen of ill fortune (tashā'amnā), because the hardship and drought that afflicts us comes from your ill omen and the ill omen of those with you.

Then He, exalted is He, made clear that among that corruption was what they intended concerning the affair of Salih (peace be upon him).

It was recited as "mahlaka" with a fatḥa on the mīm and lām, and with a kasra on the mīm... from halaka; and "muhlak" with a ḍamma on the mīm, from ahlaka. It may be a verbal noun, a place, or a time.

Then He, exalted is He, said, ﴿And they plotted a plot, and We plotted a plot, while they were unaware.﴾ Scholars have differed regarding the plotting of Allah, exalted is He, in several ways:
One: the plot of Allah is their destruction from a direction they were not aware of. It is likened to the plot of a plotter by way of metaphor. It is related that Salih (peace be upon him) had a mosque in al-Ḥijr, in a mountain pass, where he would pray. The first: concerning the explanation of hastening evil before good, there are two views:
One: when those who denied Salih (peace be upon him) found that argument did not benefit them, Salih (peace be upon him) threatened them with punishment. They said, mockingly, ﴿Bring us the punishment of Allah if you are among the truthful﴾ (Al-ʿAnkabūt: 29). At this, Salih said, ﴿Why do you seek to hasten evil before good?﴾ The meaning is: Allah has enabled you to reach His mercy and reward, so why do you turn away from that to hasten His punishment?

[Page 174]

As for describing punishment as "evil," this is a metaphor (majāz), and the reason for this figurative usage is either that punishment is among the necessary consequences of evil, or that it resembles evil in being disliked. As for describing mercy as "good," some say it is literal (ḥaqīqa) and some say it is figurative, and the first is closer to the truth.

Then, when Salih (peace be upon him) had established this true statement, they answered him with a false statement, which is their saying, ﴿We consider you a bad omen﴾, meaning: we take you as an omen of ill fortune (tashā'amnā), because the hardship and drought that afflicts us comes from your ill omen and the ill omen of those with you.

Then He, exalted is He, made clear that among that corruption was what they intended concerning the affair of Salih (peace be upon him).

It was recited as "mahlaka" with a fatḥa on the mīm and lām, and with a kasra on the mīm... from halaka; and "muhlak" with a ḍamma on the mīm, from ahlaka. It may be a verbal noun, a place, or a time.

Then He, exalted is He, said, ﴿And they plotted a plot, and We plotted a plot, while they were unaware.﴾ Scholars have differed regarding the plotting of Allah, exalted is He, in several ways:
One: the plot of Allah is their destruction from a direction they were not aware of. It is likened to the plot of a plotter by way of metaphor. It is related that Salih (peace be upon him) had a mosque in al-Ḥijr, in a mountain pass, where he would pray. The first: concerning the explanation of hastening evil before good, there are two views:
One: when those who denied Salih (peace be upon him) found that argument did not benefit them, Salih (peace be upon him) threatened them with punishment. They said, mockingly, ﴿Bring us the punishment of Allah if you are among the truthful﴾ (Al-ʿAnkabūt: 29). At this, Salih said, ﴿Why do you seek to hasten evil before good?﴾ The meaning is: Allah has enabled you to reach His mercy and reward, so why do you turn away from that to hasten His punishment?

[Page 174]

As for describing punishment as "evil," this is a metaphor (majāz), and the reason for this figurative usage is either that punishment is among the necessary consequences of evil, or that it resembles evil in being disliked. As for describing mercy as "good," some say it is literal (ḥaqīqa) and some say it is figurative, and the first is closer to the truth.

Then, when Salih (peace be upon him) had established this true statement, they answered him with a false statement, which is their saying, ﴿We consider you a bad omen﴾, meaning: we take you as an omen of ill fortune (tashā'amnā), because the hardship and drought that afflicts us comes from your ill omen and the ill omen of those with you.

Then He, exalted is He, made clear that among that corruption was what they intended concerning the affair of Salih (peace be upon him).

It was recited as "mahlaka" with a fatḥa on the mīm and lām, and with a kasra on the mīm... from halaka; and "muhlak" with a ḍamma on the mīm, from ahlaka. It may be a verbal noun, a place, or a time.

Then He, exalted is He, said, ﴿And they plotted a plot, and We plotted a plot, while they were unaware.﴾ Scholars have differed regarding the plotting of Allah, exalted is He, in several ways:
One: the plot of Allah is their destruction from a direction they were not aware of. It is likened to the plot of a plotter by way of metaphor. It is related that Salih (peace be upon him) had a mosque in al-Ḥijr, in a mountain pass, where he would pray.
