One: it is connected to what precedes it of the stories, and the meaning is: Praise be to Allah for their destruction, and peace upon His servants whom He chose, by sending them and saving them.
Two: it is a new beginning. When He, exalted is He, mentioned the conditions of the prophets (peace be upon them), and Muhammad (ﷺ) was like one who differs from those before him regarding the matter of punishment, since the punishment of total annihilation was lifted from his people, He commanded him to thank his Lord for what He had specially granted him of these blessings, and to offer peace upon the prophets (peace be upon them) who endured the hardships of the message.

As for His words, ﴿Is Allah better, or what they associate?﴾, it is a rebuke to the polytheists and a mockery of their state, because they preferred the worship of idols over the worship of Allah, exalted is He, and no rational person prefers one thing over another except for an increase in good or benefit. So this statement was addressed to them to draw attention to the extremity of their error and ignorance. It is also recited as "yushrikūna" with the yā' and with the tā' (ta'). It is related from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that whenever he recited it he would say: "Rather, Allah is better, more enduring, more exalted, and more generous."

Then know that He, glorified and exalted is He, spoke after this in a number of sections.

The First Section: Refutation of the Idol-Worshippers. The purpose of this section is to show that He, glory be to Him and exalted is He, is the Creator of the roots of blessings and their branches, so how could it be fitting to worship that from which no benefit whatsoever comes? Then He, glory be to Him and exalted is He, mentioned several kinds [of blessings]:

[Page 173]

**The third story: the story of Salih (peace be upon him)**

﴿And We certainly sent to Thamud their brother Salih, [saying], "Worship Allah." But they became two factions contending with each other.﴾ ﴿He said, "O my people, why do you seek to hasten evil before good? Why do you not ask forgiveness of Allah, that you may be shown mercy?"﴾ ﴿They said, "We consider you and those with you a bad omen." He said, "Your omen is with Allah; rather, you are a people being tested."﴾ ﴿And there were in the city nine men who spread corruption in the land and did not reform.﴾ ﴿They said, "Swear to one another by Allah that we will surely attack him and his family by night, then we will say to his heir, 'We did not witness the destruction of his family, and indeed we are truthful.'"﴾ ﴿And they plotted a plot, and We plotted a plot, while they were unaware.﴾ ﴿So see how was the outcome of their plot: that We destroyed them and their people, all of them.﴾ ﴿So those are their houses, empty because of what they did wrong. Indeed in that is a sign for a people who know.﴾ ﴿And We saved those who believed and used to be mindful of Allah.﴾

The words of the Exalted: ﴿And We certainly sent to Thamud their brother Salih, [saying], "Worship Allah." But they became two factions contending with each other.﴾ ﴿He said, "O my people, why do you seek to hasten evil before good? Why do you not ask forgiveness of Allah, that you may be shown mercy?"﴾ ﴿They said, "We consider you and those with you a bad omen." He said, "Your omen is with Allah; rather, you are a people being tested."﴾ ﴿And there were in the city nine men who spread corruption in the land and did not reform.﴾ ﴿They said, "Swear to one another by Allah that we will surely attack him and his family by night, then we will say to his heir, 'We did not witness the destruction of his family, and indeed we are truthful.'"﴾ ﴿And they plotted a plot, and We plotted a plot, while they were unaware.﴾ ﴿So see how was the outcome of their plot: that We destroyed them and their people, all of them.﴾ ﴿So those are their houses, empty because of what they did wrong. Indeed in that is a sign for a people who know.﴾ ﴿And We saved those who believed and used to be mindful of Allah.﴾

It was recited (ۤanna u'budu Allah) with a ḍamma on the nūn, following the bāʾ (the vowel of the nūn is assimilated to the following bāʾ's ḍamma), as a variant recitation (qira'a).

As for His words, ﴿then they were two factions﴾, there are two opinions:
One: the intended meaning is a believing faction and a disbelieving faction.
Two: the intended meaning is the people of Salih before any of them had believed.

As for His words, ﴿contending with each other﴾, the meaning is: those who believed only believed because they examined his proof and recognised its soundness. If that is so, there must be an opponent to those who did not accept it. And if this contention is in matters of religion, this indicates that disputation in matters of religion is valid and that it nullifies blind imitation (taqlīd).

As for His words, ﴿He said, "O my people, why do you seek to hasten evil before good?"﴾, there are two discussions.

The first: concerning the explanation of hastening evil before good, there are two views:
One: when those who denied Salih (peace be upon him) found that argument did not benefit them, Salih (peace be upon him) threatened them with punishment. They said, mockingly, ﴿Bring us the punishment of Allah if you are among the truthful﴾ (Al-ʿAnkabūt: 29). At this, Salih said, ﴿Why do you seek to hasten evil before good?﴾ The meaning is: Allah has enabled you to reach His mercy and reward, so why do you turn away from that to hasten His punishment?
Second: they were saying, out of their ignorance, that if the punishment that Salih promised befell them, as he claimed, then they would come and seek forgiveness, and then Allah would accept their repentance and avert the punishment from them. So Salih addressed them according to their own belief and said: Why do you not seek Allah's forgiveness before the punishment descends? For hastening towards good is better than hastening towards evil.

[Page 174]

The second discussion: the intended meaning of "evil" (sayyi'a) is punishment and the intended meaning of "good" (ḥasana) is reward. As for describing punishment as "evil," this is a metaphor (majāz), and the reason for this figurative usage is either that punishment is among the necessary consequences of evil, or that it resembles evil in being disliked. As for describing mercy as "good," some say it is literal (ḥaqīqa) and some say it is figurative, and the first is closer to the truth.

Then, when Salih (peace be upon him) had established this true statement, they answered him with a false statement, which is their saying, ﴿We consider you a bad omen﴾, meaning: we take you as an omen of ill fortune (tashā'amnā), because the hardship and drought that afflicts us comes from your ill omen and the ill omen of those with you.

The author of al-Kashshāf said: A man would set out on a journey and pass by a bird and drive it away; if it passed on his right (sānih), he would take it as an omen of good, and if it passed on his left (bāriḥ), he would take it as an omen of ill. When they attributed good and evil to the bird, the term was borrowed for what was actually the cause of good and evil, which is the decree and apportionment of Allah. So Salih (peace be upon him) answered with His words, ﴿Your omen is with Allah﴾, meaning the cause from which your good and your evil come is with Allah, namely His judgement and decree: if He wills, He provides for you, and if He wills, He withholds from you. It was also said: rather, the meaning is that the consequence of your ill omen from you is with Allah, which is punishment; but the first view is closer, because the people pointed to a matter that had actually occurred, so the answer must concern that matter and not something else. Then He made clear that this was their ignorance, by His words, ﴿rather, you are a people being tested﴾. It is possible that others induced them to this statement, and it is possible that the meaning is that Satan tests you through his whisperings.

Then He, glorified be He, said, ﴿And there were in the city nine men who spread corruption in the land﴾. The closer view is that the intended meaning is nine groups, since the apparent meaning of "rahṭ" is a group and not a single individual. It is possible that they were tribes, and it is possible that they were grouped under this number because of differences in their qualities and conditions, not because of differences in their cause. So Allah, exalted is He, made clear that they spread corruption in the land and did not mix that corruption with any reform, and for this reason He said, ﴿who spread corruption in the land and did not reform﴾. Then He, exalted is He, made clear that among that corruption was what they intended concerning the affair of Salih (peace be upon him).

As for His words, ﴿Swear to one another by Allah﴾, it may be an imperative, or a statement in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), with "qad" understood (ḥāl (circumstantial accusative) with an implied qad), meaning: they said, swearing to one another. And "bayāt" means attacking the enemy by night.

As for His words, ﴿then we will say to his heir, "We did not witness the destruction of his family"﴾, the meaning is: if his people accused us, we would swear to them that we were not present. It was recited as "mahlaka" with a fatḥa on the mīm and lām, and with a kasra on the mīm... from halaka; and "muhlak" with a ḍamma on the mīm, from ahlaka. It may be a verbal noun, a place, or a time.

Then He, exalted is He, said, ﴿And they plotted a plot, and We plotted a plot, while they were unaware.﴾ Scholars have differed regarding the plotting of Allah, exalted is He, in several ways:
One: the plot of Allah is their destruction from a direction they were not aware of. It is likened to the plot of a plotter by way of metaphor. It is related that Salih (peace be upon him) had a mosque in al-Ḥijr, in a mountain pass, where he would pray. They said: Salih claims that he will be done with us within three days, so we will be done with him and his family before the three days are over. So they went out to the pass and said: when he comes to pray, we will kill him; then we will return to his family and kill them. But Allah, exalted is He, sent a rock which sealed the mouth of the pass over them, so they perished, and the rest perished by the Cry.
Second: they came at night with their swords drawn, and Allah, exalted is He, had sent the angels to fill the house of Salih, and they struck them with stones; they saw the stones but did not see the one who threw them.
Third: Allah, exalted is He, informed Salih of their plot, so he took precautions against them. That is the plot of Allah, exalted is He, against them.

As for His words, ﴿that We destroyed them﴾, it is a resumptive new sentence (isti'nāf). Whoever reads it with a fatḥa (anna) treats it as a substitute for "ʿāqiba" (outcome), or as the predicate of an omitted subject whose estimate is: it (the outcome) destroys them; or he puts it in the accusative with the sense of "because we," or as the predicate of "kāna" (was), meaning: the outcome of their plot was destruction.

[Page 175]

As for His words, ﴿empty﴾ (khāwiya), it is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl), governed by what is indicated by "tilka" (those). ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar recited "khāwiyatun" with a ḍamma, as the predicate of the omitted subject. And Allah knows best.

**The fourth story: the story of Lut (peace be upon him)**

﴿And Lot, when he said to his people, "Do you commit immorality while you see?"﴾ ﴿"Do you indeed approach men with desire instead of women? Rather, you are a people who are ignorant."﴾ ﴿The answer of his people was only that they said, "Expel the family of Lot from your city; indeed they are people who keep themselves pure."﴾ ﴿So We saved him and his family, except his wife; We destined her to be among those who remained behind.﴾ ﴿And We rained upon them a rain, and wretched was the rain of those warned.﴾

The words of the Exalted: ﴿And Lot, when he said to his people, "Do you commit immorality while you see?"﴾ ﴿"Do you indeed approach men with desire instead of women? Rather, you are a people who are ignorant."﴾ ﴿The answer of his people was only that they said, "Expel the family of Lot from your city; indeed they are people who keep themselves pure."﴾ ﴿So We saved him and his family, except his wife; We destined her to be among those who remained behind.﴾ ﴿And We rained upon them a rain, and wretched was the rain of those warned.﴾

The author of al-Kashshāf said: "Mention Lot", or "We sent Lot", as indicated by "and We certainly sent to him". "Idh" (when) is a substitute (badal) on the first reading, and an adverb of time on the second.

As for His words, ﴿Do you commit immorality?﴾, it is in the form of a denunciation, even though it is worded as a question, and perhaps rebuke with such wording is more forceful.

As for His words, ﴿while you see﴾, there are several views:
One: they did not shy away from openly displaying this, in a spirit of licentiousness, and did not conceal it from one another. This is one of the reasons why this act was so grave on their part, so in rebuking them he mentioned the very thing that made the act so grave.
Two: the intended meaning is the sight of the heart, i.e., you know that it is an abomination, and you were not preceded by anyone in it, and that Allah did not create the male for the male, so it is contrary to His wisdom.
Three: you see the traces of the sinners before you and what befell them. If you say: you interpreted "see" as knowledge, and then "rather, you are a people who are ignorant"; how can they be both knowers and ignorant? I answer: he meant that you act like ignorant people in that it is an abomination while you know it; or you are ignorant of the outcome; or by ignorance he meant the frivolity and wantonness in which they were.

Then He, exalted is He, made clear their ignorance by relating that they answered this speech with something that is not fit to be an answer to it, so He said:

[Page 176]

﴿The answer of his people was only that they said, "Expel the family of Lot from your city; indeed they are people who keep themselves pure."﴾ They made the reason for their expulsion that they keep themselves pure from this foul practice, and this would necessitate that they be honoured and exalted all the more. But among the commentators some have said that they said this only mockingly. Then He, exalted is He, made clear that He saved him and his family, except his wife, and destroyed the rest. All of this has already been explained in detail. Here ends the stories in this surah, and Allah knows best.

**On Allah's address to Muhammad (ﷺ)**

The words of the Exalted: ﴿Say, "Praise be to Allah, and peace upon His servants whom He has chosen. Is Allah better, or what they associate?"﴾

On this verse there are two views:
One: it is connected to what precedes it of the stories, and the meaning is: Praise be to Allah for their destruction, and peace upon His servants whom He chose, by sending them and saving them.
Two: it is a new beginning. When He, exalted is He, mentioned the conditions of the prophets (peace be upon them), and Muhammad (ﷺ) was like one who differs from those before him regarding the matter of punishment, since the punishment of total annihilation was lifted from his people, He commanded him to thank his Lord for what He had specially granted him of these blessings, and to offer peace upon the prophets (peace be upon them) who endured the hardships of the message.

As for His words, ﴿Is Allah better, or what they associate?﴾, it is a rebuke to the polytheists and a mockery of their state, because they preferred the worship of idols over the worship of Allah, exalted is He, and no rational person prefers one thing over another except for an increase in good or benefit. So this statement was addressed to them to draw attention to the extremity of their error and ignorance. It is also recited as "yushrikūna" with the yā' and with the tā' (ta'). It is related from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that whenever he recited it he would say: "Rather, Allah is better, more enduring, more exalted, and more generous."

Then know that He, glorified and exalted is He, spoke after this in a number of sections.

The First Section: Refutation of the Idol-Worshippers. The purpose of this section is to show that He, glory be to Him and exalted is He, is the Creator of the roots of blessings and their branches, so how could it be fitting to worship that from which no benefit whatsoever comes? Then He, glory be to Him and exalted is He, mentioned several kinds [of blessings]:

**Type one: what relates to the heavens**

﴿Is He not (better) who created the heavens and the earth, and sent down water for you from the sky, and with it We caused to grow gardens of joyful beauty, whose trees you could never have made grow? Is there a god with Allah? No! But they are a people who deviate.﴾

Among its issues:

Issue one: The author of *al-Kashshaf* (al-Zamakhshari) said: The difference between *am* and *am* in ﴿am mā yushrikūn﴾ (27:59 region, "or what they associate") and ﴿amman khalaqa﴾ is that the first is *muttasilah* (connected, i.e., the sense is "which of the two is better"), whereas this one is *munqati'ah* (disconnected, in the sense of *bal*, "rather"). *Al-hadiqah* (the garden) is an orchard enclosed by a wall of *al-ihdaq*, which is encircling. It was said that *dhāt* (feminine) is used because the meaning is "a collection of gardens possessing joyful beauty," as one says "the women went." *Al-bahjah* is beauty, because the beholder is delighted by it. ﴿Is there a god with Allah? Rather,﴾ is his other, who is associated with Him and made a partner to Him. It was also read *(ilāhan ma'a Allāh)*, in the sense of "you invoke" or "you associate."

Issue two: He, exalted is He, made clear that He is the One who alone created the heavens and the earth, made the sky a place for the water and the earth a place for vegetation, and mentioned the greatest of blessings, which are the gardens possessing joyful beauty. He, exalted is He, alerted that this causing of growth in gardens is not something anyone can accomplish except Allah, exalted is He, for if any of us were able to do it, he would not need planting and patience until the fruit appears. And since He, exalted is He, is the One singled out for this favor, it is necessary that He alone be worshipped. Then He said: ﴿Rather, they are a people who deviate.﴾ People have differed regarding it. It was said: they deviate from this manifest truth. It was said: they set up others as equal to Allah. The parallel to this verse is at the beginning of Surat al-An'am.

Issue three: It may be asked: what is the wisdom of the shift (*iltifat*) in His saying ﴿fa-anbatnā﴾ ("so We caused to grow")? The answer: there is no doubt for any rational person that the creator of the heavens and the earth and the sender of water from the sky is none other than Allah, exalted is He. But perhaps doubt may arise that the one who causes the tree to grow is the human being, for a person says: "I am the one who casts the seed into the arable soil, waters it, and strives in exposing it to the sun, and the doer of the cause is the doer of the effect; so I am the one who causes the tree to grow." Since this possibility existed, he removed it, so He turned from the third-person address to ﴿fa-anbatnā﴾ and said: ﴿whose trees you could never have made grow﴾, because a person may bring the seed, the watering, the tilling, and the exposure to the sun, and then it does not come out according to his intention; and whatever happens according to his intention, he is ignorant by his nature of its essence, its measure, and its manner, so how could he be its doer? For this subtle reason the shift here is fitting.

**The second type: what relates to the earth**

﴿Is He who made the earth a resting place, and placed within it rivers, and placed upon it firmly set mountains, and placed between the two seas a barrier? Is there a god along with God? Rather, most of them do not know.﴾

The author of *al-Kashshaf* said: ﴿Is He who made﴾ and what follows it is a substitute (badal) for ﴿Is He who created﴾, so its ruling (ḥukm) is the ruling of that phrase.

Know that He, exalted is He, mentioned four benefits of the earth:

**The first benefit: that it is a resting place (qarar).** This is for several reasons:

First: He spread it out and leveled it so that it could be settled upon.

Second: He made it moderate in hardness and softness. It is not as hard as a stone, on which a person would be in pain from lying, nor as soft as water, in which one would sink.

Third: He made it dense and dusty (ghabrā) so that light could settle upon it. Had it been fine and thin, light would not have settled upon it, and had light not settled upon it, it would have become so cold that animals would die.

Fourth: He, glorified is He, made the sun's orbit tilt away from the orbit of the equatorial zone (minṭaqat al-kull), so that it sometimes moves away and sometimes comes close to the zenith of the head. Had it not been so, the seasons would not vary, and the benefits would not be obtained.

Fifth: He, glorified and exalted is He, made it still. For if it were moving, it would either be moving in a straight line or in a circle, and in either case, one could not benefit from dwelling upon the earth.

Sixth: He, glorified is He, made it a receptacle (kifāt) for the living and the dead, and He casts upon it every foul thing and brings forth from it every good thing.

**The second benefit of the earth: His saying ﴿and placed within it rivers﴾.** Know that the kinds of water that well up from the earth are four:

The first: the water of flowing springs. These arise from vapors that are abundant in matter and strong in their pressure, which burst through the earth with force, and then part of them continuously follows another part.

The second: the water of stagnant springs. These come about from vapors that have reached such strength that they burst forth onto the surface of the earth, but whose strength and abundance of matter are not enough for the following vapor to drive out the preceding one.

The third: the water of wells (qunnī) and rivers. These are produced from vapors whose strength is insufficient to split the earth. When the weight of the soil is removed from its surface, those vapors then find an outlet into which they rush with the slightest movement.

The fourth: the water of wells (ābār). These are of the spring type, like river water, except that no channel was made for it to flow to some place. The ratio of qunnī to wells is the ratio of stagnant springs. It is thus clear that were the earth not hard, those vapors would not gather within it; for were they not gathered within it, these springs would not arise on its surface.

**The third benefit of the earth: His saying ﴿and placed upon it firmly set mountains﴾.** By this is meant the mountains. We say: most springs, clouds, and mineral substances exist only in the mountains or in what is close to them. As for springs: if the earth is loose, the vapors seep out of it and no significant quantity gathers. Therefore these vapors gather only in hard earth, and mountains are the hardest of the earth. Thus they are necessarily the strongest in holding this vapor until enough accumulates to be the matter of springs. It is likely that the bed of the mountain is filled with water, and the mountain, in retaining the vapors, is like a solid alembic prepared for distillation, allowing none of the vapor to escape. The earth beneath it is like the cucurbit, the springs are like the spouts, and the vapor is like the receivers. For this reason most springs gush forth from the mountains, and fewer from the open deserts, and that lesser number occurs only when the earth is hard.

As for the fact that most clouds form over the mountains, this is for three reasons:

The first: within the mountains there is more moisture than there is in the interior of loose lands.

The second: because of their height, mountains are cooler, so there remain on their surfaces more dews and snows than remain on the backs of other lands.

The third: the rising vapors are held back by the mountains, so they do not disperse or dissolve. Once this is established, it becomes clear that the causes of abundant clouds are greater in the mountains, because the matter there is greater, both above and below, the confinement is stronger, and the dissolving cause, which is heat, is weaker. Therefore clouds are more abundant over the mountains.

As for minerals, which need vapors whose mixing with the earthly substance is greater, and which need a long period of time in which ripening is completed, nothing in this sense is like the mountains.

**The fourth benefit of the earth: His saying ﴿and placed between the two seas a barrier﴾.** The purpose of this is that sweet water should not be spoiled by mixing. Also, that one should benefit from that barrier. Also, the believer has in his heart two seas: the sea of faith and wisdom, and the sea of transgression and desire. By His grace, He placed a barrier between them so that neither would corrupt the other. Some of the wise said concerning His saying: ﴿He released the two seas, meeting each other; between them is a barrier they do not transgress﴾ (al-Raḥmān: 19–20), that when there is no transgression, ﴿there come forth from them the pearl and the coral﴾ (al-Raḥmān: 22). So when there is no transgression in the heart, religion and faith come forth through gratitude.

If it is asked: why did He make the sea salty? We say: were it not for its saltiness, it would become putrid, and the corruption of its putrefaction would spread over the earth and cause a widespread plague.

Know that the sea being located on one side of the earth rather than another is not a necessity. Rather, the truth is that the sea shifts over periods that recorded histories cannot measure, from one century to another. This is because the sea's replenishment is mostly from rivers, and rivers are mostly replenished from springs. As for rainwater, its occurrence is in one season rather than another. Then neither springs nor rainwater must have their conditions identical in the same specific places in a constant manner. Many springs dry up, and the sky often withholds rain, so at such times the valleys and rivers must dry up, and as a result the seas dry up. And when springs arise from another side, rivers arise there, and the seas come into being on that side.

Then, when He, glorified is He, made clear that He alone has power to create the earth in which these magnificent benefits exist, it became necessary that He alone deserves divinity. And by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Rather, most of them do not understand﴾ (al-ʿAnkabūt: 63), He alerted to the great ignorance of those who neglect this reflection.

The third category: what relates to the creation's need of Him, glory be to Him.

﴿Is He who responds to the distressed one when he calls upon Him, and removes the evil, and makes you successors of the earth? Is there a god with Allah? Little do you remember.﴾

This is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Is He who responds to the distressed one when he calls upon Him, and removes the evil, and makes you successors of the earth? Is there a god with Allah? Little do you remember.﴾

Know that He, glory be to Him, drew attention in this verse to two matters:

The first: His saying, ﴿Is He who responds to the distressed one when he calls upon Him﴾. The author of al-Kashshaf said: "al-darurah (necessity) is the condition that makes one need to seek refuge, and al-idtirar (being compelled) is an ifti'al (reflexive form) derived from it. One says: iḍṭarrahu ila kadhā (he compelled him to such-and-such), and the doer and the object are both mudtarr." Know that the distressed one is the one whom an illness, poverty, or one of the calamities of time has driven to humble himself before Allah, the Exalted. From al-Suddi: "the one who has no power and no strength." It was also said: the sinner when he seeks forgiveness. If it is said: He has generalized the distressed ones by His saying, ﴿Is He who responds to the distressed one when he calls upon Him﴾, yet how many a distressed person calls and is not answered? The answer: We have explained in the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh) that the definite singular noun (al-mufrad al-mu'arraf) does not indicate generality, but only indicates the quiddity (mahiyyah) alone; and a judgment affirmed of the quiddity is satisfied in its truth by its holding in a single individual of the quiddity. Moreover, He, the Exalted, promised a response, and did not mention that He responds immediately. The full discussion of the conditions of supplication and response is mentioned in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And your Lord said: Call upon Me, I will respond to you﴾ (Ghafir: 60). As for His saying, the Exalted, ﴿and removes the evil﴾, it is like an explanation of the response, for no one can remove what has befallen him of poverty into wealth, of sickness into health, or of constriction into ease, except the Capable who does not fail, and the Subduer who is not contested.

The second: His saying, ﴿and makes you successors of the earth﴾. The meaning is their inheriting its dwelling and its disposal generation after generation. By khilafah (succession) he meant possession and dominion. It is read as (yadhdhakkarun) with the ya' and with idgham (assimilation), with the ta' and with idgham, and with elision; and ma is redundant (mazidah), meaning: they remember a little remembrance. The sense is the negation of remembrance, and "little" is used in the sense of negation.

**[Type 4]:** This also concerns the needs of creation, but it is a specific need at a specific time.

﴿Is He who guides you in the darknesses of land and sea, and who sends the winds as glad tidings before His mercy? Is there a god along with Allah? Exalted is Allah above what they associate with Him.﴾

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Is He who guides you in the darknesses of land and sea, and who sends the winds as glad tidings before His mercy? Is there a god along with Allah? Exalted is Allah above what they associate with Him.﴾

[p. 180]

Know that in this verse Allah draws attention to two matters:

The first is His words: ﴿Is He who guides you﴾. The meaning is that He guides you by the stars in the sky and by the landmarks on the earth when the night covers you while you travel on land and sea.

The second is His words: ﴿who sends the winds﴾. He, glory be to Him, is the One who moves the winds, so they stir up the clouds and then drive them wherever He wills. If it is objected: "We do not grant that He is the One who moves the winds, for the philosophers (al-Falasifa) said: the winds are only generated from smoke. Not all smoke is the black body rising from what has burned in fire; rather, every earthly body that rises by the heating action of warmth, whether the warmth is the heat of fire or the heat of the sun, is smoke." They said: the generation of winds from smokes occurs in two ways:

One of them is the more common, and the other is less common. As for the more common, it is that when many smokes rise upward, upon reaching the cold layer, either their heat is broken by the coldness of that air, or it is not broken. If it is broken, it inevitably becomes heavy and descends, and from its descent the air is set in motion, and so wind arises. If its heat is not broken by the coldness of that air, it must continue to ascend until it reaches the sphere of fire, which moves with the motion of the celestial sphere. At that point it cannot ascend further because of the motion of the fire, so those smokes turn back and become wind. It may be said: if the impulse of these smokes were due to the motion of the high air, their motion would not be downward but toward the direction of the motion of the high air. We answer this objection in two ways:

One of them: the configuration of the upward rising of those smokes, and the configuration of the matter's adhesion to them, may cause them to move in a direction opposite to the direction of the moving obstacle. This is like an arrow that strikes a moving body, which sometimes turns it toward its own direction if the obstructor is able to deflect the moving body from its course, and it is also able to turn it toward the direction of its own motion; and sometimes it turns it in the opposite direction, when the separating force is able to restrain but not to deflect.

The second: sometimes the upward rising of some smokes from below prevents the descending smokes from above from sinking down; for this reason the motion spreads to all sides. Know that the people of Islam have two positions here:

The first is to establish the proof of the invalidity of this cause, and its explanation is in two ways:

The first: the smoky particles are earthly, so they are heavier than the vaporous watery particles. Then, when vapor cools, it descends in a straight line as rain. So when smoke cools, why does it not descend in a straight line, but instead goes right and left?

The second: the motion of those particles downward is natural, and their motion to the right and left is accidental (ʿaraḍiyya). The natural is stronger than the accidental, and if it is not stronger, it is at least not less than equal. Moreover, when wind moves right and left, it may be strong enough to uproot trees, throw down walls, and even mountains. So when those smoky particles move with their natural motion, which is downward, they must destroy the ceiling. Yet we see much dust descending from the air and falling upon the ceiling without its descent being felt, let alone its destroying it. Thus the falsity of what they mentioned is established.

The second position: Suppose the matter is as they described. Nevertheless, the efficient causes and the receptive causes of these things are created by Allah, glory be to Him and exalted. For if it were not for the sun and its effect in raising vapors and smokes, and if it were not for the layers of air, these events would not have occurred. It is known that whoever establishes causes which lead to wondrous benefits and profound wisdoms, that Establisher is the One who brought about those benefits. Therefore, in every case, these matters must bear witness to a wise Governor who is necessary in His essence (wājib li-dhātih), thereby cutting off the chain of needs.

**[p. 181]**

**The Fifth Type: What Concerns the Gathering and Resurrection**

﴿Is He who originates creation and then repeats it, and who provides for you from the heaven and the earth? Is there a god with Allah? Say: Bring your proof, if you are truthful.﴾

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Is He who originates creation and then repeats it, and who provides for you from the heaven and the earth? Is there a god with Allah? Say: Bring your proof, if you are truthful.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, enumerated the blessings of this world, He followed that with the blessings of the Hereafter by His saying: ﴿Is He who originates creation and then repeats it﴾, because the blessings of the Hereafter in the form of reward are not complete except by the repetition after the initial creation and by reaching the limit of legal responsibility (taklif). Thus the speech includes all these blessings. It is known that they are not complete except by provisions, so He said: ﴿and who provides for you from the heaven and the earth﴾. Then He said: ﴿Is there a god with Allah?﴾, denouncing what they were upon. Then He made clear by His saying: ﴿Say: Bring your proof, if you are truthful﴾ that there is no proof for you. Thus they are falsifiers. This indicates that a claim必 requires ... [sic: "lā budda fī al-da'wā min" followed by "wa 'alā fasād al-taqlīd"]; that is, a claim requires a proof, and this indicates the corruption of blind imitation (taqlid). If it is said: how was it said to them, ﴿Is He who originates creation and then repeats it﴾, when they denied the repetition? The answer: they acknowledged the initial origination, and the indication of the initial origination for the repetition is a clear and strong indication. When the speech was accompanied by a clear indication, it became as though they had no excuse left for denial. Here ends the last of the mentioned proofs for the perfect power of Allah, exalted is He.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 27, verses 65–66:

Allah, may He be exalted, says: ﴿Say: None in the heavens and the earth knows the unseen except Allah, and they do not perceive when they will be resurrected.﴾ ﴿Rather, their knowledge has culminated concerning the Hereafter. Rather, they are in doubt about it. Rather, they are blind to it.﴾

Know that when He, may He be exalted, made clear that He alone holds power, He likewise made clear that He alone holds knowledge of the unseen. And when this is established, it is established that He is the God who is worshipped, because the God (ilah) is the One from whom it is valid to recompense whoever deserves reward, in a manner that does not mix with the people of punishment. If it is said: the rule of the exception (istithna') is that it removes what would otherwise have been included, so that it must be, or must be valid, that it falls under the excepted term. And this verse indicates the exception of Allah, glorified and exalted be He, from those in the heavens and the earth. Therefore it must be that He is among those in the heavens and the earth, and this necessitates that He is in a place. The answer: this verse has an apparent meaning that is abandoned, because whoever says that He, exalted be He, is in a place claims that He is above the heavens, and whoever says that He is not in a place has declared Him far above all places. Thus it is established by consensus that He, exalted be He, is not in the heavens and the earth. Therefore it is necessary to interpret it. So we say: He, exalted be He, is among those in the heavens and the earth, just as the theologians say: Allah, exalted be He, is in every place, in the sense that His knowledge is in all places. It is not said that His being in the heavens and the earth is metaphorical while their being in them is literal, and that it is not permissible for a speaker to intend one expression both literally and metaphorically, because we say: their being in the heavens and the earth, just as it is actually realized, namely the presence of their essences in spaces, is likewise realized metaphorically, namely their being aware of those places. So when we carry this "being in" (ghaybah) on the metaphorical meaning, which is being in them in the sense of knowledge, the Lord, glorified and exalted be He, and the servants are both included in it, and so the exception is valid.

As for His saying: ﴿and they do not perceive﴾, it is a description of the people of the heavens and the earth, denying that they have knowledge of the unseen. He mentioned among the unseen matters the time of resurrection with His saying: ﴿when they will be resurrected﴾. So "ayyana" means "when" (mata), and it is a compound word from "ay" and "al-an," which is the time. It has also been read as "iyyana" with a kasra on the hamzah.

As for His saying: ﴿Rather, their knowledge has culminated concerning the Hereafter﴾, know that the discussion of the author of "al-Kashshaf" on it is arranged under three investigations:

The first investigation: there are twelve readings for it: bal adraka, bali ddaraka, bali iddarak, bal tadaraka, bal a'adraka with two hamzahs, bal aadraka with an alif between them, bal aadraka with lightening and transposition, bala ddaraka with a fatha on the lam and shaddah on the dal. Its original form is bal addaraka in interrogative form. Bala adraka, bala a'adraka, am tadaraka, am adraka.

The second investigation: idarraka is originally tadarraka, the taa' being assimilated into the dal, and addaraka is ifta'ala.

The third investigation: the meaning of iddaraka 'ilmuhum is that it reached its end and became complete, while adraka means it followed in succession and became firm. Then there are several aspects:

One: the causes of the firmness and completion of knowledge are that the Resurrection is certainly coming, without doubt, and it has come to them, and they were enabled to know it, yet they are doubters and ignorant. This is His saying: ﴿Rather, they are in doubt about it. Rather, they are blind to it.﴾ It refers to the polytheists among those in the heavens and the earth, because since they were among them, their act is attributed to all of them, as one says: "The sons of so-and-so did such-and-such," when in fact only some of them did it. If it is said: the verse was brought to establish that Allah, exalted be He, alone has knowledge of the unseen, and that servants have no knowledge of any of it, and that the time of their resurrection is among the unseen, which they do not perceive, then how does this meaning fit with describing the polytheists as denying resurrection despite the firmness of the causes of knowledge and their ability to know? The answer: it is as if He, glorified be He, said: how can they know the unseen when they doubt the existence of the Hereafter, the reality of which the manifest and overpowering proofs have indicated? So whoever is heedless of this manifest matter, how can he know the unseen, which is the most hidden of things?

Two: describing them with the firmness of knowledge is a mockery of them, as one says to the most ignorant of people, "How knowledgeable you are!" as a jest, and this is because they doubted the establishment of what the path to it is clear and evident.

Three: adraka may mean "ended and perished," from your saying: "adrakat al-thamarah" (the fruit has ripened and is ready to be picked), because that is its final point, at which it ceases to exist. Al-Hasan explained it as "their knowledge has vanished." And tadaraka is from "tadaraka banu fulan" when they followed one another into destruction. As for the reading of whoever read "bal a'adraka" as an interrogative, it is an interrogative in the manner of denial of their attainment of knowledge; likewise for whoever read "am adraka" and "am tadaraka," because "am" there is the one that means "bal" together with the hamzah. As for whoever read "bala adraka," since He brought "bala" after His saying: ﴿and they do not perceive﴾, its meaning is "bala, they perceive," then He explained the perception by His saying: "their knowledge has reached its end concerning the Hereafter," in the manner of mockery, whose meaning is emphasis in negating knowledge. It is as if He said: their perception of the time of the Hereafter is that they do not know its occurrence, which returns to negating perception in the most emphatic way. As for whoever read "bala a'adraka" as an interrogative, its meaning is: "bala, they perceive when they will be resurrected," then He denied their knowledge of its occurrence, and since their knowledge of its occurrence is denied, no perception of the time of its occurrence is attained by them. If you say: what is the meaning of these three transitions? I say: they are nothing but a clarification of their degrees. He first described them as not perceiving the time of resurrection, then as not knowing that the Resurrection is coming, then as wallowing in doubt and misgiving, then with what is worse in condition, which is blindness. In this there is a subtle point: He, exalted be He, made the Hereafter the starting point of their blindness, and therefore He used "min" rather than "'an," because thought is directed to the outcome, and the recompense is what made them like cattle.

He stated (exalted is He): When He spoke about the state of origin, He then spoke about the state of return. This is because doubt about the Return arises only from doubt about His complete power or His complete knowledge. Once it is established that He, exalted is He, is capable of all possibilities and knows all that is known, it follows that He can distinguish the parts of each accountable person's body from the parts of another's body, and that He is able to restore their composition and life to them. And once the possibility of this is established, the validity of the doctrine of the Gathering (al-Hashr) is established. When God had explained these two foundations in the verses before this one, He naturally did not repeat them in this verse. Instead, He related that they marvelled at being brought forth alive after they had become dust, and they attacked it from two angles:

The first: their saying, ﴿Indeed we and our fathers were promised this before; this is nothing but the fables of the ancients.﴾ That is: this is a statement, just as it was said to us, so it was said to those before us, and no trace of it has appeared. Therefore it is, in their view, among the fables of the ancients, meaning: what is not sound of reports.

If it is asked: Here He mentioned ﴿we and our fathers were promised this﴾, and in another verse, ﴿we and our fathers were promised this﴾ with the order changed. What is the difference? We say: placing something first indicates that the thing placed first is the primary intended meaning, and that the speech was directed for its sake. Furthermore, since He, exalted is He, had already shown the proof for these two foundations, and it is evident that whoever comprehends both of them recognises the truth of the Gathering and the Resurrection, it follows that they turned away from these proofs and did not reflect upon them. The cause of that turning away was love of this world, love of leadership and status, and not submitting to others. Therefore He confined Himself to showing that this world is transient and perishable, and said: ﴿Say: travel through the earth and observe how was the end of the criminals.﴾ On this there are two questions:

[Page 184]

First question: Why did He not say "how was the end of the criminals" (kānat, feminine)? Its answer: because its feminine marker is not real (ḥaqīqī), and because the meaning is "how was the final outcome of their affair."

Second question: Why did He not say "the end of the disbelievers"? Its answer: the purpose is that warning should be achieved for all the sinners. Then, exalted is He, He consoled His Messenger regarding what he suffered from these disbelievers, saying: ﴿And do not grieve over them, and do not be in distress because of what they plot.﴾ Thus He combined the removal of grief from him over their disbelief with the removal of fear from their side, and this was like a guarantee of supporting him against them. His saying ﴿and do not be in distress﴾ means: in a constriction of the heart. It is said: the thing became constricted (ḍāqa shay'un ḍayqan wa ḍīqan), with fatḥa and kasra. Ḍayq is a lightened form of ḍayyiq. It is also permissible that the meaning be: in a difficult matter arising from their plotting.

The second angle, concerning the disbelievers: their saying ﴿When is this promise, if you are truthful?﴾ indicates that they mentioned it by way of mockery. God answered with His saying: ﴿It may be that some of what you are hastening will follow you (radifa lakum)﴾, and that is the punishment of the Day of Badr. The lām was added for emphasis, like the bā' in ﴿and do not cast yourselves by your own hands into destruction﴾ (al-Baqarah: 195). Or the verb was given the sense of a verb that takes the lām, as in dana lakum and azifa lakum, and its meaning is: it followed you and overtook you. Al-A'raj read (radifa lakum) with the pattern of dhahaba, and both are dialects, though the kasra (radifa) is more eloquent. Here there are two discussions:

The first discussion: 'asā (perhaps) and la'alla (perhaps) in the promise and threat of kings indicate the certainty of the matter. They mean by this only to display their dignity, and that they do not hasten to vengeance, being confident that their enemy cannot escape them. Upon this manner the promise and threat of God proceed.

The second: It has been established by rational proofs that the punishment of being veiled (ʿadhāb al-ḥijāb) is more severe than the punishment of the Fire. For this reason He said: ﴿No! Indeed they, that Day, will be veiled from their Lord. Then indeed they will be those who burn in Hell.﴾ (al-Muṭaffifīn: 15–16). So He placed the veiling before the Hellfire. Moreover, they were veiled in the present, so the full cause of the punishment was already present, except that preoccupation with the world and its pleasures acts as an obstacle preventing the perception of that pain, just as when a numb limb is touched by fire, the cause of the pain is present at the moment, but the sensation of that pain does not arise because of the obstacle. When the obstacle is removed, the affliction becomes great. Likewise here: when the body is removed, the punishment of the veiling becomes great. Thus His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It may be that some of what you are hastening will follow you﴾ means that what necessitates it and what effects it is present, and its completion will occur only after death. Then, exalted is He, explained the reason for not hastening the punishment, saying: ﴿And indeed your Lord is full of bounty toward mankind﴾. Bounty (faḍl) is beneficence, and its meaning is that He is bestowing favour upon them by delaying the punishment. But most of them do not recognise this blessing nor give thanks for it. This verse refutes the view of those who say that there is no blessing of God upon the disbelievers. Then He, exalted is He, made clear that He is aware of what is in their hearts, saying: ﴿And indeed your Lord knows what their breasts conceal and what they disclose.﴾

Here there is a rational discussion: He placed what their breasts conceal before what they disclose in knowledge. The reason is that what their breasts conceal are the motives and intentions, and these are causes of what they disclose, which are the actions of the limbs. Knowledge of the cause is a cause of knowledge of the effect. This is the reason for that ordering. (The verb) was read as tukinnu (تُكِنُّ), it is said: kanantu al-shay' and akmantuhu, when I concealed it and hid it. He means that He, exalted is He, knows what they hide and what they disclose of enmity toward the Messenger and their schemes.

It is also permissible that these be adjectives, with the tā' there for intensification, like the rāwiyah in their saying: "Woe to the poet because of the rāwiyah of evil." It is as if He, exalted is He, said: there is no thing of intense concealment and obscurity except that God knows it and encompasses it, and has recorded it in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawḥ al-Maḥfūẓ). Then, exalted is He, explained the reason for not hastening the punishment, saying: ﴿And indeed your Lord is full of bounty toward mankind﴾. Bounty (faḍl) is beneficence, and its meaning is that He is bestowing favour upon them by delaying the punishment. But most of them do not recognise this blessing nor give thanks for it. This verse refutes the view of those who say that there is no blessing of God upon the disbelievers. Here there is a rational discussion: He placed what their breasts conceal before what they disclose in knowledge. The reason is that what their breasts conceal are the motives and intentions, and these are causes of what they disclose, which are the actions of the limbs. Knowledge of the cause is a cause of knowledge of the effect. This is the reason for that ordering. It is as if He, exalted is He, said: there is no thing of intense concealment and obscurity except that God knows it and encompasses it, and has recorded it in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawḥ al-Maḥfūẓ). This is because doubt about the Return arises only from doubt about His complete power or His complete knowledge. Instead, He related that they marvelled at being brought forth alive after they had become dust, and they attacked it from two angles:

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 27, verses 76–81:

Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, this Qur'an relates to the Children of Israel most of that over which they differ.﴾ ﴿And indeed, it is guidance and mercy for the believers.﴾ ﴿Indeed, your Lord will judge between them by His ruling, and He is the Mighty, the Knowing.﴾ ﴿So rely upon Allah; indeed, you are upon the manifest truth.﴾ ﴿Indeed, you cannot make the dead hear, nor can you make the deaf hear the call when they turn away, retreating.﴾ ﴿And you cannot guide the blind out of their error. You can only make hear those who believe in Our verses, so they are Muslims [submitting].﴾

Know that when He, glorified is He, finished speaking about establishing the Origin (al-mabda') and the Return (al-ma'ad), He then mentioned what relates to prophethood (al-nubuwwah). Since the greatest pillar in establishing the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ) is the Qur'an, Allah, exalted is He, first explained that it is a miracle (mu'jizah) in several respects:

The first: The narratives mentioned in the Qur'an agree with what was mentioned in the Torah and the Gospel, while it is known that he (peace be upon him) was unlettered (ummi), that he did not associate with any of the scholars, and that he never occupied himself with seeking benefit or learning. Therefore, this could only be from Allah, exalted is He. They differed: some said that He meant by it what they differed over and disagreed about; others said He meant by it what some of them had distorted (harrafa); and some said: rather, He meant by it the reports of the prophets. The first is closer.

The second: His saying: ﴿And indeed, it is guidance and mercy for the believers.﴾ This is because some people said: "When we contemplated the Qur'an, we found in it rational proofs for monotheism (al-tawhid), the Gathering (al-hashr), and prophethood, and an explanation of the attributes of Allah, exalted is He, and a description of the qualities of His majesty, which we did not find in any of the books. We also found its legislations (al-shara'i') agreeing with and conforming to the intellects, and we found it free from contradiction and incoherence. So it was guidance and mercy from these aspects. We also found human faculties incapable of compiling a book in this manner, so we knew that it is nothing but from Allah, exalted is He. Thus the Qur'an is a miracle from this aspect."

The third: That it is guidance and mercy for the believers, owing to its reaching such eloquence (fasahah) that they were unable to oppose it, and that is a miracle. Then, when He, exalted is He, explained that it is a miracle indicating the prophetic mission (al-risalah), He mentioned after it two matters:

The first: His saying: ﴿Indeed, your Lord will judge between them by His ruling, and He is the Mighty, the Knowing.﴾ The meaning is that although the Qur'an relates to the Children of Israel most of that over which they differ, do not be held captive by them, for your Lord is the One who judges between them, that is, between the right and the wrong among them. This is like a warning to the disbelievers. Therefore He said: ﴿And He is the Mighty﴾, that is, the All-Powerful who cannot be prevented, ﴿the Knowing﴾ of what He judges, so it will only be the truth. If it is said: qada' (judgment) and hukm (ruling) are one thing, so His saying ﴿judge between them by His ruling﴾ is like saying "judges by His judgment" and "rules by His ruling." The answer: the meaning of His saying ﴿by His ruling﴾ is by what He rules, which is His justice, since He judges only with justice; or He meant by His ruling, and what supports this is the reading of those who read (bi-hikamihi), the plural of hikmah (wisdom).

The second: After the manifestation of the proof of His prophetic mission, He commanded him to rely upon Allah and not turn toward the enemies of Allah, and to proceed with the affairs of the mission with a strong heart. So He said: ﴿So rely upon Allah﴾. Then He justified that with two matters:

One of them: His saying: ﴿Indeed, you are upon the manifest truth.﴾ In it is an explanation that the one who is upon truth deserves the support of Allah, exalted is He, and that he will not be forsaken.

The second: His saying: ﴿Indeed, you cannot make the dead hear.﴾ It is only fitting to make this a cause for the command to rely upon Allah because, as long as a person hopes to take something from someone, his heart does not have the strength to show opposition to him. When he cuts off his hope from him, his heart becomes strong enough to show his opposition. Allah, glorified and exalted is He, detached Muhammad (ﷺ) from them by explaining to him that they are like the dead, like the deaf, and like the blind, so they do not understand, do not hear, do not see, and do not turn to any of the proofs. * * *

As for His saying: ﴿And on the Day when We gather from every nation﴾, know that this is among the events that occur after the Hour has arisen. The difference between the first "min" and the second is that the first is partitive (lil-tab'id) and the second is explanatory (lil-tabyin), like His saying: ﴿from the idols﴾ (al-Hajj 22:30).

As for His saying: ﴿so they will be driven in ranks﴾, its meaning: their first is held back for their last until they all gather, and then they are thrown into the Fire. This is an expression for the abundance of their number and the spread of its extremities, just as the armies of Sulayman were described with this.

As for His saying: ﴿until, when they arrive, He will say, "Did you deny My signs"﴾, although this may include the miracles of the messengers, as some have said, the intended meaning is all the signs, so it includes all the disbelievers who denied all the signs of Allah or some of them.

As for His saying: ﴿without comprehending them in knowledge﴾, the "waw" is for the circumstantial state (lil-hal), as if He said: "Did you deny them, at first sight, without reflection or consideration that would lead to a comprehensive knowledge of their reality?"

As for His saying: ﴿or what was it that you were doing?﴾, the meaning is: since you did not occupy yourselves with that important work, then what work were you doing after that? As if He said: every other work is as though it were not work. Then He said: ﴿And the Word will fall upon them﴾, meaning that the promised punishment overtakes them because of their denial of the signs of Allah, and it preoccupies them from speaking and making excuses, as in His saying: ﴿This is a Day when they will not speak﴾ (al-Mursalat 77:35). Then, after He frightened them with the conditions of the Resurrection, He, glorified is He, mentioned a statement that is suitable to be a proof of monotheism (tawhid), of resurrection, and of prophethood, as an emphasis in guiding to faith and preventing disbelief. So He said: ﴿Have they not seen that We made the night for them to rest therein and the day giving sight?﴾

[p. 187]

As for how it indicates monotheism: since it is clear to reason that the alternation from light to darkness, and from darkness to light, does not occur except by a compelling and exalted power. As for how it indicates resurrection: since the power of Allah, exalted is He, over turning this form from light to darkness and the reverse has been established, then what impossibility is there in the establishment of His power over turning life into death once, and death into life again? As for how it indicates prophethood: since He, exalted is He, alternates the night and the day for the benefit of those under obligation, and in sending prophets and messengers to creation there are great benefits, then what prevents sending them to creation for the sake of achieving those benefits? It is established that this single statement is sufficient to establish proof for the validity of the three foundations from which their disbelief arises and their deserving of punishment.

Then there are two questions concerning the verse:

The first question: What is the reason that sight was attributed to the day, when it belongs to its people? The answer: to draw attention to the perfection of this attribute in it.

The second question: When He said: ﴿He made the night for you to rest therein﴾ (Yunus 10:67), why did He not say: "and the day for you to see therein"? The answer: because rest in the night is the purpose of the night, whereas seeing in the day is not the purpose, but rather a means to bringing religious and worldly benefits.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿Indeed in that are signs for a people who believe﴾, He singled out the believers for mention, although they are proofs for everyone, since they alone are specified with acceptance and benefit, as has preceded in its like.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 27, verses 82–86:**

Indeed in that are signs for a people who believe.﴾

Know that Allah, exalted is He, demonstrated with compelling proofs the perfection of power and the perfection of knowledge. Then He based upon these two the statement that resurrection (al-hashr) is possible. Then He explained the aspect in which the Qur'an is a miracle (i'jaz), and based upon that the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ). Then He now speaks about the preliminaries of the Hour. He delayed speech on this subject until after establishing prophethood, because these matters cannot be known except through the word of the truthful Prophet, and this is the height of excellence in ordering. Know also that He, exalted is He, mentions at times what serves as a sign of the Hour, and at other times the events that occur at the Hour. He first mentioned, among the signs of the Hour, the beast of the earth. The people have spoken about it from several aspects:

The first: concerning the size of its body. In a hadith, its length is sixty cubits. It is also narrated that its head reaches the clouds. From Abu Hurayrah: the distance between its two horns is a farsakh for a rider.

The second: concerning the manner of its creation. It is narrated that it has four legs, down and feathers, and two wings. From Ibn Jurayj in its description: the head of an ox, the eye of a pig, the ear of an elephant, the horn of a stag, the chest of a lion, the color of a leopard, the flank of a cow, the tail of a ram, and the hoof of a camel.

The third: concerning the manner of its emergence. From Ali, peace be upon him, that it emerges over three days while the people look on, and only a third of it emerges. From al-Hasan: its emergence is not complete until after three days.

The fifth: concerning the number of its emergences. It is narrated that it emerges three times: it emerges from the far end of Yemen, then it lies hidden, then it emerges in the desert, then it lies hidden for a long age. Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 27, verse 87:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And on the Day the Horn is blown, whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth will be terrified, except whom Allah wills. And all will come to Him humbled.﴾

Know that this is the second sign of the establishment of the Resurrection (al-Qiyamah).

As for His saying, ﴿And on the Day the Horn is blown﴾, there are several views:

The first: the Horn is something resembling a trumpet, and Israfil, peace be upon him, blows into it by the permission of Allah, Exalted is He. When people hear that sound, which is so intense that their natures cannot bear it, they will be terrified by it, will swoon, and will die. This is like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So when the trumpet is sounded﴾ (al-Muddaththir: 8). This is the view of the majority.

The second: it is possible that it is a metaphor for the call of death, for their emergence from their graves is like the emergence of an army at the sound of the instrument.

The third: that al-Suwar (the Horns) is the plural of al-Surah (the form), and they took the blowing into it to be the blowing of the spirit. The first view is closer, because the apparent meaning indicates it, and nothing prevents it.

As for His saying, ﴿And whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth will be terrified﴾, know that He said fa-fazi'a (then were terrified) and did not say fa-yafza' (then will be terrified), to indicate the certainty and establishment of the terror, and that it is undoubtedly going to occur. For the past tense verb indicates that the action exists and is definite. The intended meaning is their terror at the first blast.

As for His saying, ﴿except whom Allah wills﴾, the intended meaning is: except those whom Allah has made firm of heart among the angels. They said they are Jibril, Mika'il, Israfil, and the Angel of Death. It was also said: the martyrs. It is narrated from al-Dahhak: the Houris, the guardians of the Fire, and the bearers of the Throne. It is narrated from Jabir that Musa is among them, because he swooned once. A similar statement is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And the Horn will be blown, and whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth will swoon, except whom Allah wills﴾ (al-Zumar: 68). There is no definitive report on this, and the Book only indicates the general meaning.

As for His saying, ﴿And all will come to Him humbled﴾, it was read as atawhu and atahu, and as dakhirin and dakhirin, and as dakhirin. The plural is according to the meaning, and the singular is according to the wording. Al-dakhir and al-dakhar mean the humbled, the abased. It was said: the meaning of "coming" is their presence at the place of standing after the second blast. It is also possible that it means their return to the command of Allah and their submission to Him.

Page 189

قَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿And you see the mountains, thinking them fixed, while they pass by as the clouds pass. [It is] the handiwork of God, who perfected everything. Indeed, He is Aware of what you do.﴾.

Know that this is the third sign of the Hour's coming, namely the moving of the mountains. The reason they are thought to be fixed is that when large bodies move swiftly, in one direction and in one manner, the observer supposes them to be standing still, even though they are passing with rapid motion.

As for His words, ﴿handiwork of God﴾, it is one of the emphatic verbal nouns (al-masadir al-mu'akkidah, nouns of the verb used to stress its meaning), like His words ﴿God's promise﴾ (al-Fath: 29) and ﴿the colouring of God﴾ (al-Baqarah: 138). However, its emphasized verb is omitted, and it is the governing verb (al-nasib) for ﴿and on the day the Trumpet is blown﴾. The meaning is that, since He had mentioned these matters, which no one other than Him is able to do, He made this handiwork among the things He perfected and brought about in accordance with wisdom and correctness.

Al-Qadi Abd al-Jabbar said: "In this there is an indication that ugly things are not part of His creation, for otherwise they would have to be described as perfected. But consensus (ijma', the agreement of the scholars) prevents this." The answer is that perfection (al-itqan) occurs only in composite things (al-murakkabat), so it is impossible to describe accidents (al-a'rad, attributes that inhere in substances) with it. And God knows best.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 27, verses 89–90:**

The Exalted said: ﴿Whoever comes with a good deed, for him there is better than it, and they will be safe from the terror of that Day.﴾ ﴿And whoever comes with an evil deed, their faces will be thrown into the Fire. Are you recompensed except for what you used to do?﴾

Know that when the Exalted spoke about the signs of the Hour, He then explained the states of the accountable (al-mukallafun) after the Hour has come. The accountable person is either obedient or disobedient. As for the obedient, he is the one who came with a good deed, and for him there are two matters.

The first: for him there is something better than it, and that is the reward. If it is objected: the good deed that the servant brought includes knowledge of God the Exalted and sincerity in acts of obedience, while the reward is only eating and drinking. How then is it permissible to say that eating and drinking is better than knowledge of God? Its answer is in several respects:

[p. 190]

The first: the reward of theoretical knowledge (al-ma'rifah al-nazariyyah) attained in this world is the necessary knowledge (al-ma'rifah al-darurriyyah) attained in the Hereafter, and the pleasure of gazing upon His noble Face, glorified and exalted is He. The proofs have indicated that the most noble of felicities is this pleasure. If the verse is not taken to mean this, it would follow that eating and drinking are better than knowledge of God the Exalted, and that is false.

The second: the reward is better than the deed in that the reward is everlasting and the deed is finite; and because the deed is the act of the servant, whereas the reward is the act of God the Exalted.

The third: ﴿for him there is better than it﴾ means: for him there is a good that comes from it, and that is Paradise.

The second question: al-hasanah (the good deed) is a singular noun with the definite article, and it has been established that it does not denote generality; rather, the realization of it is sufficient with the occurrence of a single instance. Since this is so, let us interpret it as the most perfect of good deeds in status and the highest in rank, which is faith (al-iman). Therefore Ibn 'Abbas said: among the instances of the good deed is the word of testimony (kalimat al-shahadah). This would necessitate the certainty that the people of faith will not be punished. Its answer: that good is that their punishment will not be eternal.

The second matter for the obedient is that they are safe from every terror. This is not as some have said, that the terrors of the Hour encompass both the believer and the disbeliever. If it is objected: Did not He say at the beginning of the verse: ﴿so whoever is in the heavens and whoever is in the earth will be terrified﴾? How then does He negate terror here? Its answer: the first terror is that which no one is free from upon perceiving a severe event, and it comes suddenly out of awe and dread, even if the doer of good is safe from that harm reaching him, as it is said: a man enters with a fearful heart and a trembling soul, even if it is an hour of honor and dignity.

As for the second, it is the fear of punishment.

As for the reading of the one who recited ﴿min faza'in﴾ with tanwin (nunation on faza', i.e., "from a terror"), it admits of two meanings: from a single terror, which is the fear of punishment; and as for what befalls a person of awe and dread upon witnessing the terrors, no one is free from it, and there are reports that indicate this; and from a terror of extreme severity that cannot be described, which is the fear of the Fire. And amina (to be safe) is transitive by the preposition and directly, as in His saying: ﴿Did they then feel secure from the plan of God? But none feels secure from the plan of God﴾ (al-A'raf: 99).

This is the explanation of the state of the obedient. As for the explanation of the state of the disobedient, it is His saying: ﴿And whoever comes with an evil deed﴾. It has been said: the evil deed is associating partners with God. His saying: ﴿their faces will be thrown into the Fire﴾: know that the whole person is sometimes expressed by the face, the head, and the neck, so it is as if it were said: they will be thrown into the Fire headlong, like His saying: ﴿so they will be thrown headlong﴾ (al-Shu'ara': 94). It is also permissible that the mention of the faces is an indication that they will be cast into it prone upon their faces.

As for His saying: ﴿Are you recompensed except for what you used to do?﴾, it permits iltifat (a shift in grammatical address), and the reporting of what will be said to them at the time of their being cast down, by the implied verb of saying (idmar al-qawl).

Know that when He, glorified and exalted, had explained the origin (al-mabda', the beginning of creation), the return (al-ma'ad, the afterlife), prophethood (al-nubuwwah), the preliminaries of the Resurrection, and the description of the people of the Resurrection regarding reward and punishment, and this is the complete scope of what relates to clarifying the fundamentals of the religion, He concluded the discourse with this subtle conclusion, saying: "Say, O Muhammad, indeed I have been commanded with things:

[p. 191]

The first: that I have been commanded to single out God alone for worship and not to take any partner with Him.
